slides.title: Three days on dark mode, five minutes on the parcel ID
slides.tldr: Teams pour days into decisions that could wait and settle expensive ones in five minutes, because they never learned to tell which is which.

blocks.body: Ryan's team started a package delivery app. In the first sprint, one developer spent three days on dark mode: a second set of colors, a toggle in settings, and fixes for the screens that looked wrong in it. It was nice to have, but no customer had asked for it yet. The parcel ID took five minutes: just use the database's auto-incrementing 1, 2, 3. A year later they found that anyone could open another person's parcel by typing the next number, and a rival could count Ryan's daily volume the same way. An ownership check closed the first leak in an afternoon. Hiding the volume needed IDs nobody can guess, which meant changing the ID type, and by then the old one was printed on hundreds of thousands of receipts, built into the mobile app and stored in three partners' systems. Five more minutes at the start, weighing auto-increment against a random ID, would have saved three months.

blocks.caption: What each decision cost to add or change a year later

items.label: Dark mode
items.tip: The same three days in any month: no stored data or partner depends on it, so waiting costs nothing. Yet it went first.

items.label: Logging library
items.tip: It touches a few places in the code, but nobody outside notices, so the effort ends within days.

items.label: Parcel ID type
items.tip: A five-minute decision. Changing it meant running old and new IDs side by side for months.

blocks.body: The decision that will cost the most to change deserves the most thought.

aside.title: Why did the ID take three months?
aside.body: Old mobile apps still send the numeric ID, and you can't force everyone to update. Partners had stored the old IDs in their own databases. And you can't recall a printed receipt. So both kinds of ID had to run side by side while everything moved over slowly.

items.meaning: Long arguments over trivial, easy topics, because everyone understands them and so everyone has an opinion.
The time, money and risk it takes to change a decision later.

check.q: What was the real mistake in Ryan's team: choosing the ID type, or how they spent their time?
check.a: How they spent their time. They gave three days to something that would cost the same three days at any later time, and five minutes to something that took three months to change, without considering any alternative.

slides.title: The touchstone: what will it cost to change later?
slides.tldr: Three questions tell you if a decision is architectural: how much stands on it, whether data has piled up, and whether outsiders use it.

blocks.title: Six floors on a two-floor foundation
blocks.body: Ryan built his house with a foundation sized for two floors. Ten years later he wanted six, and the engineer said the whole thing would have to come down. Yet he had changed the window shutters, the flooring and the paint as often as he liked. The foundation is expensive because everything else stands on it.

blocks.title: Spotting a foundation with three questions
items: **How much stands on it?** The more code, teams and systems depend on it, the more a change costs.
**Has data piled up?** Stored data must be poured into the new mould, which is far harder than changing code.
**Does anyone outside your control use it?** You can't force an old mobile app or a partner to change.

blocks.body: Architecture represents the significant design decisions that shape a system, where significant is measured by cost of change.

aside.body: Ask yourself: "A year from now, how many days will changing this take, and who will I have to convince?"

items: A decision confined to one file is cheap; the wider it spreads, the more it costs.
The same decision is cheap on day one and expensive two years later, because a lot has been built on it since.
This is a judgment aid, not a calculator. "Days or months?" is precise enough; don't spend a meeting estimating.

items.label: Is there a door back, or not?

check.q: What are the three questions for telling whether a decision is architectural?
check.a: How much stands on it, whether data has piled up, and whether someone outside your control uses it. The more "yes" answers, the more a change costs.

slides.title: Four familiar foundations — and the things that are just paint
slides.tldr: Stop for the database choice, the data model, service boundaries and the public API contract; move fast on most other decisions.

blocks.body: In almost every project, four kinds of decision behave like foundations. When you face one, stop, think through at least two alternatives and write down your reason. Most other decisions are like window grilles and paint: let one person decide and the team moves on.

blocks.caption: The four foundations: why they're hard to change

cells: Every query and all stored data is tied to its shape
rows.tip: Changing it means rewriting every query and moving all the data from one database to another.

cells: Millions of rows must be poured into a new mould
Money as float or as integer cents
rows.tip: Which tables, which columns, which types, how they relate. Once data piles up, fixing a mistake here is the most painful.

cells: Code, data and teams all get re-split
Orders and payments together or apart
rows.tip: Where the system is cut into pieces. Cut in the wrong place and every feature has to touch both pieces.

cells: External clients aren't in your hands
rows.tip: A promise to the outside world. Once someone writes code against it, you can't change it alone.

blocks.title: These are paint — no long meetings
items: Variable, method and folder names — the IDE changes them in a minute.
Code formatting — let `php-cs-fixer` handle it.
The internals of a class — nobody outside sees them.
A library hidden behind an interface — changing it means changing one class.
A few more are often foundations: language and framework, the login method, and how you keep many customers' data apart in one system.
Write the reason for a foundation decision on one page ([[thinking/documentation/nobody-remembers-why|ADR]]) — in six months someone will ask, "Why did we do this?"
Stopping has a price too. For a throwaway prototype you plan to bin, skip the ceremony: the cost of change never comes due.

check.q: What are the four familiar architectural decisions, and what do they share?
check.a: Database choice, data model, service boundaries and the public API contract. In all four, either stored data or someone else's dependency is involved.

slides.title: Sorting a feature's decisions
slides.tldr: List every decision in the feature and put its cost of change beside it: minutes, days, weeks, months. Spend your time only on weeks and months.

blocks.body: When a new feature arrives, first list all its decisions, then write the cost of changing each one later. Take the "parcel tracking" feature in the package delivery app. Below is Ryan's team's list: only three of the seven are foundations, so those three got the whole review meeting.

blocks.caption: Seven decisions of the "parcel tracking" feature, sorted by cost

cells: Months — spreads to receipts and partners
rows.tip: Part of the public contract. Once it's in a customer's hands, you can't take it back.

cells: Months — partners are out of your hands
rows.tip: Another company will write code against it. Even removing one field later would break their system.

cells: Which table holds status, and its shape
rows.tip: The data model. Thousands of status rows pile up every day, so a wrong shape gets costlier every day.
If SMS sending sits behind an interface, switching company means rewriting one class.
Only one Vue component uses it, so the impact of a change stops at that one file.
The IDE's rename changes them safely. One comment in review is enough.
One line of CSS. If it's wrong, the next deploy fixes it.

blocks.title: A five-minute routine
items: Write all the feature's decisions in one list.
Put the cost of change beside each: minutes, days, weeks or months.
For every "weeks" and "months" entry, write two alternatives and a reason, and get a review.
Let one person decide the rest and move on — fixing a mistake later is cheap.

aside.body: Minutes or days: decide alone. Weeks or months: stop, write it down, show it.

items: Giving every decision equal time, leaving no time for the three that matter.
Saying "we'll see later" and making a foundation decision without thinking.

check.q: Why did choosing the SMS company land under "days" rather than "months"?
check.a: Because the SMS-sending code sits behind an interface. Switching company means rewriting one class; the rest of the code, the data and outsiders never notice.

slides.title: Turning paint into a foundation by accident
slides.tldr: Return an entity as JSON and your table columns become the public contract; a separate response class keeps the inside cheap to change.

blocks.body: The best-known mistake: returning a Doctrine entity straight from a controller as JSON. Every column name then becomes part of the public API. Renaming a column used to be as cheap as repainting; now it breaks the mobile app, which means the paint itself has turned into a foundation. The fix: a separate response class for whatever leaves the system.

marks.tip: The database id is now part of the URL. Change the id type and every old link and client breaks.
Rename a column tomorrow, or add a secret one, and it goes straight to every client.
Clients see only these three fields — that is the contract. Change the table however you like; as long as this class stays put, nobody breaks.
`{trackingCode:parcel}` means: look up the Parcel by its trackingCode property using the URL value. The internal id no longer leaks out.
The response class is sent, not the entity. The internal structure and the outside promise are now separate.

blocks.body: Keep the inside structure and the outside promise separate, and the inside stays as cheap as paint.

aside.body: A cheap decision turns expensive on its own when many things lean on it directly. A thin layer in between stops the shock of a change right there.

items: When two separate apps read the same table directly, the whole schema becomes the contract between them.
When a vendor's SDK classes spread through the code, switching vendor goes from "days" to "months".

use: Anything that leaves the system: a public API, a partner feed, a mobile app's responses
avoid: A screen only your own team uses: the extra class and mapping code buy nothing there

items.label: Changing an API without breaking the contract
Hexagonal: keeping outside things at arm's length

check.q: Why does returning an entity as JSON make renaming a column expensive?
check.a: The column name is now an API field. Mobile apps and partners wrote code against that name, so renaming it breaks everything of theirs, and their code isn't in your hands.

slides.title: An hour on a banner color, one minute to drop a column
slides.tldr: Teams spend time on decisions that are easy to undo, and rush through the ones that can't be undone.

blocks.body: Sarah's team got two jobs in one week: pick the homepage banner color, and drop the old `phone` column from the database. The banner took an hour of the weekly meeting, with everyone giving an opinion. The column was dropped in one minute, with a single migration and no backup. The next day they learned that the phone numbers of older customers existed only in that column.

blocks.caption: Two kinds of door: one you can walk back through, one you can't

columns.title: A door you can return through
items: Changing the banner color
Turning on a new feature flag
Adding a column
If it goes wrong, one deploy restores the old state
columns.tip: If you get it wrong, you walk back through and try again. A mistake is cheap, so speed is the asset here.

columns.title: A one-way door
items: Dropping a column or table
Removing a field from a public API
Sending money or an email to a customer
If it goes wrong, there's no way back
columns.tip: Once you're through, there's no coming back. A mistake is costly and permanent, so go slowly and verify.

aside.title: The email that couldn't be recalled
aside.body: A team once sent an "offer ended" email to production addresses instead of the test database. They fixed the code within an hour, but an email can't be called back. The only option was to apologize with another email.

items.meaning: A small script, run once, that changes the database structure, for example adds or drops a column.
Putting a new version of the code on the live server.
A saved copy of the data that you can restore if something gets deleted.
The doorway other companies' apps use to talk to yours. You can't see or fix their code.

check.q: Where did Sarah's team go wrong in dividing their time?
check.a: An hour went to a banner that is easy to undo, while dropping a column that can't be undone took one minute with no safety net.

slides.title: Which kind of door is it — and how fast to move
slides.tldr: Decide reversible things fast; decide irreversible ones slowly and in writing. The cost of going back is what tells them apart.

blocks.title: Renting a flat versus buying land
blocks.body: If you don't like a rented flat, you give notice at month-end and leave, so deciding quickly is fine. But once you've bought land and built a house, there's no way back, so you check the deed, the plan and the neighbors before buying. In software, some decisions are rented flats and some are land purchases.

blocks.caption: Software decisions: which kind of door each one is

cells: Turning on a new feature flag
Switch the flag off and you're back
rows.tip: The code is already there; you're only flipping a switch. No retreat is cheaper than this.
If the column is nullable (or has a default), old code doesn't notice it, so nothing breaks. Adding is safe; deleting is dangerous.

cells: With an interface, change one class
rows.tip: The rest of the code knows only the interface, so switching company means rewriting one class.
Without a backup the data is gone for good. Before any delete, ask: who still reads this?
Outside apps wrote code against this field. Remove it and their apps break, and that's out of your hands.

cells: Emailing, texting or paying a customer
rows.tip: Once a message is out, it can't be pulled back. So verify the address and the environment before sending.

blocks.body: Move fast on what you can reverse; on what you can't, go slowly, in writing, with a second pair of eyes.

aside.body: One question: "If I'm wrong, how do I get back, and at what cost?" If the answer is "one click", go ahead; if it's "I can't", stop.

items.meaning: A decision you can easily reverse if it turns out wrong.
A decision that is hard or impossible to reverse once made.

check.q: Adding a column versus dropping one: which is which kind of door, and why?
check.a: Adding is a two-way door, because old code doesn't notice and you can drop it later. Dropping is one-way, because data doesn't come back without a backup.

slides.title: Turning a one-way door into a two-way door
slides.tldr: Hide a big decision behind an interface and a feature flag, so you can go back to the old code path if it goes wrong. The flag does not undo data.

blocks.body: Some decisions look one-way but can be made two-way. Don't scatter a vendor's SDK through your code. Keep it behind an `interface` (a contract that says what can be asked, not who answers), and keep the new path behind a **feature flag** (an on/off switch read from configuration). Then changing one class or flipping the flag brings the old path back. The flag restores code, not data: whatever the new path already wrote stays written.

blocks.caption: Same switch of SMS company, with and without an interface

columns.title: SDK called everywhere
items: 30 files call the company's SDK directly
Switching company: edit and retest all 30
Nobody dares try the new company
columns.tip: Every file that sends an SMS knows the company's classes. The dependency is spread, so leaving is a big job.

columns.title: Behind SmsGateway
items: 30 files call the SmsGateway interface
Switching company: write 1 new class
Keep the old class and going back is one line
columns.tip: The 30 files know only the interface. The company hides in one adapter class, so the dependency is in one place.

marks.tip: The rest of the code knows only this interface. It doesn't need to know which company sends the SMS.
#[AsAlias] says: when someone asks for SmsGateway, hand them this class. Switch company and only this one line moves.
The `bool:` env processor turns "true"/"1" into a real bool. The flag comes from the environment and isn't hard-coded.
Both paths live side by side. If the new one misbehaves, turn the flag off and you're back on the old path.

items: Create interfaces for things that are external (SMS, payments, file storage), not for every class.
Write a removal date next to every flag. Old flags piling up become the new clutter.
An env var is read when the process starts, so flipping it means a restart or deploy. For an instant switch, store the flag in the database.
Two paths mean double the tests, and they cost real effort. Use this for risky, hard-to-reverse changes, not for every small edit.

items.label: Hexagonal: keeping outside things at arm's length

check.q: If the new SMS company turns out to be bad, what has to change in the code to go back to the old one?
check.a: Only the class that the interface is aliased to. All the other code knows SmsGateway, not the company.

slides.title: The drop-column trap: four steps instead of one
slides.tldr: Changing code and dropping a column in one deploy cuts off your way back; remove it in four steps: expand, migrate, switch, contract.

blocks.body: Sarah's team made one mistake: changing the code and dropping the column in the same deploy. When a bug showed up in the new code, going back to the old code didn't help, because the column was gone. The fix is to make the drop the very last step, in its own deploy, once you're certain nobody reads the column any more.

marks.tip: The data is gone for good, instantly. If you find a bug and go back to the old code, this column won't come back.
down() restores the column's structure, not its data. The column returns, but empty.

blocks.caption: Four steps to remove a column safely, each its own deploy

steps.title: 1. Expand
steps.body: Add a new `mobile_number` column. Old code notices nothing.
steps.tip: Adding alone is a two-way door. Nothing can break in this step.

steps.title: 2. Migrate
steps.body: Copy data from the old `phone` into the new column, and write to both.
steps.tip: Because both columns are written, any code version finds correct data, so you can step back at any time.

steps.title: 3. Switch
steps.body: Make the code read only the new column. Watch for a while to see that all is well.
steps.tip: The old column is still intact, so if something's wrong, going back to the previous code version is enough.

steps.title: 4. Contract
steps.body: Once sure, and with a backup, drop the old `phone` column.
steps.tip: The only one-way step. Up to here, the other three steps kept your way back open.

blocks.body: Deleting always comes last, in its own deploy, with a backup.

aside.body: Break a one-way job into several small, reversible steps, and the risk piles up only in the last one. The rest are cheap and safe.

check.q: Why does the drop step go last, in its own deploy?
check.a: Because it's the only one-way step. In every earlier step the old column stays intact, so you can safely go back if the code has a problem.

slides.title: Expand and contract, in real code
slides.tldr: Step 1-2 is one additive migration plus a dual write in the entity; the drop waits for its own deploy and a zero-row check.

blocks.body: Back to Sarah's team. The first migration only adds `mobile_number` and copies the old numbers into it, so the "older customers" never exist only in one column. It can be undone, because `down()` just drops the new column and `phone` is untouched.

marks.tip: On a table with millions of rows, copy in batches instead. One huge UPDATE can lock the table and stall live traffic.
Zero rows means every old number exists in the new column. Only now is the one-way step safe to take.

blocks.body: Between deploy 1 and deploy 4 the code must keep both columns in step. While the old and new code versions run side by side, either may read, so every write goes to both.

marks.tip: The old column stays correct, so rolling back to the previous code still finds the right number.
Reads prefer the new column. Once the zero-row check passes for a while, the fallback and the old column can go.

use: Any column or table that real data lives in
avoid: Scratch data in a dev database: just drop it
A tiny internal table you can rebuild in minutes: four deploys cost more than the risk

items: The price: four deploys instead of one, and for a while two columns that must stay equal.

check.q: Before the final drop, which query proves no number would be lost, and what result do you need?
check.a: Count rows where phone is not null but mobile_number is null. You need 0, and a backup, before dropping phone.

slides.title: A loan taken in the Black Friday rush, with interest six months later
slides.tldr: A rushed job left unfixed piles up like a loan, and the interest is that every new feature gets a little slower.

blocks.body: Ryan's team built a Black Friday offer feature in three days. There was no time, so they copied the old checkout code and half-edited it. Black Friday sales were great and everyone was happy. But since then, every change to checkout has to be made in two places, and one of them is often forgotten.

blocks.caption: Time to build a feature of the same size, month by month

items.label: Before Black Friday
items.tip: The code was clean then, so a change went in one place only.

items.label: After month 1
items.tip: The copied code has to be changed in two places, so the work grew a little.

items.label: After month 3
items.tip: Time goes on hunting bugs in the forgotten copy and double-checking every change.

items.label: After month 6
items.tip: Nobody is sure what breaks where they touch, so everyone moves slowly out of fear.

blocks.body: Tech debt doesn't come free. You pay in interest, as extra time on every feature.

aside.title: The corner store's tab book
aside.body: When a store owner lets regulars run a tab, sales go up, and it can be a smart move. But if the tab book isn't kept, nobody remembers who owes what. The debt stops being a debt and becomes lost money.

check.q: The feature shipped in three days with copied code. Where do you pay the "interest"?
check.a: On every later change. The same work is done in two places, mistakes happen and checking takes time, so each feature gets a little slower.

slides.title: Two kinds of debt: knowing and unknowing
slides.tldr: Debt taken on knowingly, with a repayment plan, is a tactic; debt that piles up unnoticed or ignored is the real danger.

blocks.title: A bank loan versus a loan shark
blocks.body: Taking a bank loan to grow your business is smart: you know the amount, the interest and the installments up front. But borrow from a loan shark without working it out and the interest just keeps growing. Code debt is the same: taken knowingly and written down, it's a loan; allowed to pile up unknowingly, it's a trap.

blocks.caption: The four boxes of tech debt: deliberate or inadvertent, prudent or reckless

cells: "Now I see there was a better way back then"
rows.tip: Both are normal. In the first you borrowed knowingly; in the second, what you learned made the old code look dated.

cells: "No time for design, just make it work"
rows.tip: This is the dangerous row. In the first, everyone knows and nobody thinks about repaying; in the second, nobody even knows the debt exists.

blocks.title: Three conditions for good debt
items: You know the amount: exactly which shortcut you took is written down.
You know the interest: what gets harder if you don't fix it is stated.
There's a repayment date: who will fix it, when, and how much time they get.

aside.body: Borrowing isn't the sin. Not writing it down and forgetting to repay is.

items.meaning: The work you must do now to fix the shortcut.
The extra time and risk each change costs until the shortcut is fixed.
A fixed work cycle, usually 1 or 2 weeks, after which the team plans the next one.

use: A real deadline with real value, such as the Black Friday sale, and a debt you can write down
avoid: Shortcuts in security, money or data-integrity code: there the interest is paid in incidents, not in extra days
Any shortcut you cannot give a repayment date

check.q: When is tech debt a good tactic, and when is it a trap?
check.a: A tactic when taken knowingly, written down, with a repayment date. A trap when it piles up unknowingly or ignored, or when nobody thinks about repaying.

slides.title: The debt ledger: where to write it and how
slides.tldr: Write a one-page entry for each debt: what, why, interest, repayment terms and date; leave a marker with a ticket number in the code.

blocks.body: To manage debt, you first have to write it down. A plain file or a list of tickets is enough, as long as each entry answers four questions: what, why, how much interest, and when it will be repaid. If you write a `TODO` in code, include the ticket number, or nobody will ever find it.

blocks.code:
- id: DEBT-12
  what: 'Copied checkout for Black Friday: the two services are nearly identical'
  why: 'Three-day Black Friday deadline, no time for design'
  interest: 'Every checkout change goes in two places, 2-3 extra bugs a month'
  repay: 'Merge them into one class and separate the differences with a strategy, about 3 days'
  owner: 'Ryan'
  due: '2027-02-01'
  trigger: 'Before the third campaign'

marks.tip: Writing the interest means counting the cost of the debt. Leave it out and nobody will see why repaying matters.
Without an owner and a due date an entry is just a complaint. Put a name and a date on it.
A marker with the ticket number. One grep finds every debt in an instant.
When the date passes, the test goes red. That's a harsh tactic, so keep it for important debts and agree it with the team.

items: Keep each entry to one page; nobody reads long essays. Use a short, regular template like an ADR.
At the start of each sprint, spend 5 minutes on the register: which debts have passed their date?

items.meaning: One tracked job in your task board, with a number, so it can be found and assigned.
Architecture Decision Record: a one-page note saying what was decided and why.
A command that searches text in files. `grep -r DEBT- src/` lists every marker.

check.q: Which four questions should each entry in the debt ledger answer?
check.a: Which shortcut was taken, why, what the interest (cost) is if it stays unfixed, and how and when it will be repaid, and by whom.

slides.title: Three habits for paying off debt
slides.tldr: Fix small debts whenever you touch them (boy scout rule), set aside time each sprint for big ones, and pick the debt with the highest interest.

blocks.body: "Drop everything and rewrite" isn't a way to repay debt. Old code holds years of small bug fixes and rules that nobody wrote down; a rewrite silently drops many of them, and it always runs longer than planned. Pay in small installments instead. Leave the code a little cleaner wherever you touch it, reserve some time for debt in every sprint, and repay the debt with the highest interest first.

marks.tip: The magic number got a name. Five minutes of work, but the next person won't have to guess.

blocks.caption: Splitting a 10-day sprint: a separate instalment for debt

items.label: New features
items.tip: The core business work. Most of the time goes here.

items.label: Debt repayment
items.tip: A regular instalment every sprint. A big debt gets repaid in small pieces.

items.label: Buffer
items.tip: For surprise bugs and urgent work. Without one, debt time is the first thing to get cut.

blocks.body: Whatever file you touch, leave it a little cleaner than you found it.

use: If a debt hurts every week, repay it first.
Repay debt in the code you change often before the rest.
avoid: Don't fix code nobody ever touches just because it's ugly.

items.meaning: Changing how code is organized without changing what it does.
A bare number in code whose meaning is a secret, like 5000. Give it a named constant.

items: Big refactoring without tests: you introduce new bugs while repaying. The next slide shows the test to write first.
Pushing debt time to "next sprint" again and again.

check.q: Which debt do you repay first: code you change every week, or code you change once a year?
check.a: The one you change every week. Interest is paid each time you touch the code, so the more it's touched, the costlier the debt there.

slides.title: Repaying DEBT-12: merge the copy into one class
slides.tldr: Pin today's totals with a test, then merge the two classes: the one real difference becomes a small injected policy, and the shared rules live once.

blocks.body: Here is what the Black Friday copy cost. In January the sales tax rate was updated to 8% in `CheckoutService`, and nobody remembered `BlackFridayCheckoutService`. Black Friday orders kept being taxed at the old 7%.

marks.tip: The January fix landed here only.
Same job, written twice. This copy was forgotten, so every Black Friday order was charged the old rate.

blocks.body: The repayment has two moves. First write a test that sends one fixed cart through both classes and records today's totals, so the merge cannot change behavior by accident. Then keep a single `CheckoutService` and turn the only real difference, the Black Friday discount, into a small swappable piece: a **strategy**, an object that answers one question.

marks.tip: When the campaign ends, point this at a NoDiscount class. One line changes, and no copy exists to forget.
The shared rule is written once. The next tax change touches one place.

use: The same change has already been made in two places more than once
avoid: Two pieces of code that only look alike but change for different reasons: merging couples them
Code nobody touches: it pays no interest, so leave it

items: Merging without the pinning test: you cannot tell whether the totals still match.
Making the policy too general. One difference needs one small interface, not ten options.

check.q: Why write a test before merging the two checkout classes, and what should it record?
check.a: To prove the merge changes nothing by accident. It sends one fixed cart through both classes and records today's totals, then must stay green.

slides.title: A team of 10, 12 services
slides.tldr: A small team that splits into 12 services on day one gets none of the benefits, only the extra burden of networks, deploys and debugging.

blocks.body: A startup with 10 developers wanted to be "modern", so in the first month they split the app into 12 services. Now a single "place order" request passes through five services. When one is slow, everyone is slow, and finding where the bug is takes hours. The developers spend more time on the glue between services than on features.

blocks.caption: From one app to twelve services: what changed

columns.title: A single app
items: One method call, in microseconds
One deploy, one log
Data stays consistent in one transaction
You can run the whole thing on your own machine
columns.tip: A method call inside one process is fast and safe, and you can understand the whole app at once.

columns.title: 12 services
items: Five calls in a row, each 99.9% reliable: about 5 orders in 1,000 fail instead of 1
12 deploys, 12 logs, 12 places to look
Transactions break; reconciling data is hard
12 containers in Docker just to run the system
columns.tip: Each network call between services is slow, can fail, and needs extra code.

blocks.body: Microservices solve an organizational problem, not a code problem. With a small team, there is no such problem.

aside.title: The wedding kitchen
aside.body: For a 200-guest wedding, the cooks in one big kitchen work side by side, talk, and share the salt and pepper. Split that same job into 12 small kitchens and each has to coordinate by phone, and if one runs late, the whole meal is late.

items.meaning: A small separate app that does one job and talks to the other services over the network.
Putting a new version of the app on the live server.
A group of database changes that either all happen or none do.

check.q: Why is starting a small team with 12 services trouble?
check.a: Every call crosses the network, so it's slower and more fragile, and deploys, logs and data reconciliation all multiply by twelve, yet you get none of the benefit of separate teams.

slides.title: Three shapes: monolith, modular monolith, microservices
slides.tldr: A monolith is one lump, a modular monolith has separate rooms in one house, and microservices are separate houses; the real difference is how firm the boundaries are.

blocks.title: A hall, flats and separate homes
blocks.body: A monolith is one big hall where everybody can touch everything. A modular monolith is separate flats in one building: there are walls, you go in through a door, but the foundation and roof are shared. Microservices are separate homes, where getting from one to another means crossing the road.

blocks.caption: Comparing the three shapes

rows.tip: A modular monolith still has one deploy. That's what spares you the complexity of microservices.
The problem with a monolith isn't being a monolith, it's having no boundaries. A modular monolith brings boundaries back.

cells: One, each module owns its tables
rows.tip: In a modular monolith, reading another module's tables directly is forbidden; you ask through that module's API.
In a modular monolith, calls are still cheap and safe. The network cost comes only with microservices.
Team size is the biggest factor. Independent deploys only pay off when you have independent teams.

aside.body: A monolith isn't bad by itself. A monolith without boundaries is.

items.meaning: The code for one business capability, with its own data and a public door.
Split into services, but coupled so tightly they can't be deployed except together.

check.q: What is the main difference between a modular monolith and microservices?
check.a: A modular monolith has boundaries but runs as one process with one deploy. In microservices every boundary crosses the network and is deployed separately.

slides.title: Building a modular monolith in Symfony
slides.tldr: Under src/, make a folder per business capability, give each an Api interface, and hold only IDs, not other modules' entities.

blocks.body: In a modular monolith, each folder under `src/` is one business capability. Every module has exactly one public door, the interfaces in its `Api/` folder. Other modules call those interfaces, never the internal entities or repositories. And instead of making a Doctrine relation to another module's entity, keep only its ID.

blocks.code:
src/
  Billing/
    Api/BillingApi.php             <- the only file others call
    Domain/Invoice.php
    Infrastructure/DoctrineInvoiceRepository.php
  Shipping/
    Api/ShippingApi.php
    Application/ScheduleDelivery.php
    Domain/Delivery.php
  Catalog/
    Api/CatalogApi.php
    Domain/Product.php

marks.tip: The public door. Everything outside it is internal to the module, and nobody outside may touch it.
Shipping doesn't know which classes Billing has. It knows only the BillingApi interface.
Linking by ID means that even if Billing becomes a separate service later, nothing in Shipping's tables will change.

items.desc: Catches any module calling another module's internal classes

items: A `ManyToOne` to another module's Doctrine entity leaves the boundary existing only in the folder name.
Don't return entities from an Api interface; return small DTOs or plain values.

check.q: What goes wrong if the Shipping module has a `ManyToOne` to Billing's Invoice entity?
check.a: The two modules become tied to the same table structure. A change inside Billing breaks Shipping, and splitting them into services later becomes close to impossible.

slides.title: The shortcut that quietly ends the modular monolith
slides.tldr: A Doctrine relation or a repository call across modules ties them together. Keep only an ID, ask through the Api, and let a tool fail the build on shortcuts.

blocks.body: The shortcut is tempting. Shipping needs to know whether an order is paid, so it links straight to Billing's `Invoice`. It works today. But now Shipping depends on Billing's table and on its internal status text, so a change inside Billing breaks Shipping, and Billing can never become its own service. Doing it properly costs a little discipline: one more interface, and a tool that fails the build when someone takes the shortcut.

marks.tip: A Doctrine relation into another module. Rename a Billing column and Shipping's mapping breaks too.
Shipping now knows that Billing stores the status as the text "paid". Billing can't change that without checking Shipping.
Only the ID is stored. Billing can rename its tables or become a service, and this column stays the same.
The paid question is asked through BillingApi, so Billing stays free to answer it however it likes.

items: Run `vendor/bin/deptrac analyse` in CI, so a shortcut like the first one fails the build instead of getting through review.

items.meaning: A tool that reads your code and fails when one folder uses another folder it is not allowed to.

check.q: What does Shipping store about a Billing order, and how does it learn whether the order is paid?
check.a: It stores only the order ID, and asks `BillingApi::isPaid()` through the public door. It never links to Billing's entity or reads its status text.

slides.title: Where to draw boundaries, and when to split into services
slides.tldr: Draw boundaries by business capability and data ownership, not by technical layer; split into a service only when you need a separate team and separate scaling.

blocks.body: Draw a boundary in the wrong place and every feature has to touch two or three modules. Two questions keep boundaries right: which business capability is this (payments, delivery, catalog), and who owns this data? Splitting by technical layer, such as a "database service", is completely the wrong way.

blocks.caption: Good and bad ways to draw boundaries

columns.title: By business capability
items: Billing, Shipping, Catalog
Each is the sole owner of its data
Others ask only through the public API
A new feature usually lands in one module
columns.tip: A feature usually falls within one business capability, so changes stay inside one module.

columns.title: By technology
items: ControllerService, DatabaseService
Everyone writes to the same tables
One feature means changes in every service
Separate services, but deployed together
columns.tip: Every feature passes through every layer, so a single change touches every service.

blocks.title: Check before splitting into separate services
items: A separate team wants to deploy without waiting for others.
This part has scaling or security needs very different from the rest.
The boundary has held steady in the modular monolith for months, not moving around.
You have people to carry the cost of running it (monitoring, CI, data reconciliation).

blocks.body: Build a modular monolith first. Cut only once the boundaries have proven durable, and only if you have a reason.

use: Modular monolith: most new projects and small to mid-sized teams.
Microservices: many teams that need separate scaling and separate releases.
avoid: Splitting into services only because "everyone does it" or for your CV.

items.meaning: Adding servers when load grows. One part, like image resizing, may need ten servers while the rest needs one.
The automatic build-and-test step that runs on every code change.
Dashboards and alerts that tell you a service is slow or down.

check.q: Which two questions are most useful when drawing service boundaries?
check.a: Which business capability is this, and who is the sole owner of this data? When the answers are clear, the boundary lasts and changes stay inside one module.

slides.title: A 600-line controller: afraid to change the discount rule
slides.tldr: When HTTP, SQL, business rules and email are mixed in one controller, even a tiny rule change means understanding the whole file.

blocks.body: In Ryan's app, the whole order job lives in one controller: reading the JSON, running SQL, calculating the discount and sending the email. The rule is "10% off above $100", and the same rule is needed in another API and an admin page. It is trapped inside the controller, so Ryan copies it into each. Six months later first orders get 15% off. He updates two copies and forgets the third, so a first order of $120 is charged $102 while the admin page shows $108.

marks.tip: The HTTP job: reading the request. That does belong in a controller, but nothing more than that.
A business rule. If it's needed elsewhere you have to copy it, and copies never stay identical.
Raw SQL. Rename the table and the controller breaks too.

aside.body: With four kinds of work in one file, you can't change, test or reuse any one of them separately.
The more files you must touch to change one rule, the less tidy the code.

check.q: What happens when the discount rule lives in the controller and another API needs it?
check.a: You copy it, and when the rule changes later, every copy has to be changed separately. Forget one and two places show two different prices.

slides.title: Three layers, and one direction of dependency
slides.tldr: The controller knows only HTTP, the service holds business rules, the repository fetches and stores data; and dependencies run only from top to bottom.

blocks.title: The restaurant's waiter, cook and storeroom
blocks.body: The waiter takes the order and delivers the food, but doesn't cook. The cook knows the recipes but doesn't know the customer's table. The storekeeper only fetches and stores ingredients and knows no recipes. Because the three jobs are separate, you can change the waiter (from a delivery app to phone orders) and the cook's cooking doesn't change.

blocks.caption: Three layers, top to bottom

layers.label: Controller
layers.tip: The waiter. Only takes input, calls the service and shapes the reply. No business rules here.

layers.label: Service / Use case
layers.sub: Business rules: discounts, checks, sequence of work
layers.tip: The cook. The real rules live here, and it knows nothing of HTTP or SQL.

layers.label: Repository
layers.tip: The storekeeper. This layer knows how data is obtained (Doctrine, SQL), not the rules.

layers.label: Database
layers.tip: At the very bottom. Everything above leans on it, but it knows nobody.

blocks.title: What each layer must not know
items: The service knows no `Request` or `Response`, because the rules stay the same even if HTTP changes.
The repository knows no discounts or business rules.
The controller writes no SQL and calculates no rules.

blocks.body: Dependencies run only downward. A lower layer never knows the layer above it.

items: Testing shows if the layers are right: if a service test needs an HTTP request, the layering is wrong.

check.q: Which layering rule breaks when a service takes a `Request`?
check.a: The dependency went from bottom to top: a business rule now knows HTTP. Then the same rule can't be used from a console command or a queue handler.

slides.title: Arranging three layers in Symfony
slides.tldr: The controller only binds a DTO and calls a service; the service runs the rules and uses a repository interface, with Doctrine underneath.

marks.tip: The validation rules sit in the DTO. No if-else needed in the controller.
The controller just calls one service and shapes the reply. That is its whole job.
First orders get 15%, whatever the amount. The new rule lives here and nowhere else.
Above $100 (10,000 cents) the discount is 10%. Everything else gets none.
products and orders are interfaces. The Doctrine versions live in the layer below, and this class never sees them.
The service asks DiscountPolicy for the total, so it holds no discount rule of its own. Callers 2 and 3 do the same.
No email here. A separate handler listening for OrderPlaced sends it, so this class has no HTTP and no mailer.

blocks.caption: One $120 first order, before and after the rule moved

columns.title: Before: three copies
items: Checkout updated to 15%: charges $102
Admin page missed the change: shows $108
The same order shows two different prices
columns.tip: Each place calculated the discount on its own, so each had to be updated by hand.

columns.title: After: DiscountPolicy
items: The rule lives in one class, with its own test
Checkout, the other API and the admin page all call apply()
The next change touches one file, and all three agree
columns.tip: One class holds the rule, and every place asks it.

items: Name services by the job they do (`PlaceOrder`, `CancelOrder`), not vague names like `OrderManager`.
One job per service makes tests easier to write.

items.meaning: Data Transfer Object: a plain object that only carries data, here the checked fields of the request.
A message saying something has already happened, like OrderPlaced. Anyone interested listens and does its own job.

use: A rule needed in two or more places, or one that changes often.
avoid: A one-off check used in a single place: a private method is enough.
The price: one more class to find and to keep tidy.

items.label: Putting work for later on a queue

check.q: Why is sending the email split out through an event instead of living in the `PlaceOrder` service?
check.a: Placing the order and emailing are two separate jobs. Kept apart, changing one doesn't touch the other, and a slow email doesn't slow the order down.

slides.title: Moving off legacy: the strangler fig, piece by piece
slides.tldr: Put a router in front of the old app without shutting it down, move one path at a time to new code, and delete the old code at the end.

blocks.title: A new bridge beside the old one
blocks.body: You can't close a busy bridge for repairs. So a new bridge is built alongside, and traffic is moved over one lane at a time. Once the new lane works, the old lane is torn down. Moving off legacy is the same: a router goes in front, and traffic shifts path by path.

blocks.caption: The same rewrite, two ways: what the calendar looks like

columns.title: Rewrite it all at once
items: Plan: 6 months. Reality: 14, because the old app kept getting fixes
Nothing reaches users in all that time
Launch day: hidden rules, like no cash on delivery above $400, are missing
Orders go wrong, so the team rolls back: 14 months, nothing shipped
columns.tip: How a big-bang rewrite typically ends. The numbers are an illustration, not a statistic.

columns.title: Strangler fig
items: Week 1: a router goes in front. Nothing changes for users
Week 2: /orders moves to the new app with one nginx line
A bug appears: remove the line and the old path is back in seconds
Every week ships something real, and you can stop at any point
The price: two apps to run for months, and shared data to handle with care
columns.tip: Small, reversible steps, each one already in front of real users.

blocks.caption: The router sits in front and sends /orders to the new app

nodes.label: User
nodes.tip: The user has no idea there are two apps behind the scenes.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.tip: The heart of the strangler. Change one line here and a path moves from old to new.

nodes.label: Old app
nodes.tip: It shrinks over time. The code for any path that has moved can be deleted from here.

nodes.label: New Symfony app
nodes.tip: Rewritten code for each moved path lives here. It keeps growing.

edges.label: The user sends requests to the same address as before
/orders and anything else that has moved go to the new app
All other paths still go to the old app

marks.tip: Moving a path is this one line. If there's trouble, remove the line and the old path is back.

blocks.title: The steps
items: Put a router in front of the old app; behavior must not change.
Pick one small, low-risk path and rewrite it.
Run the two side by side for a while and compare the answers.
Shift the traffic, then delete the old code.

items.meaning: A tree that grows up the trunk of an old tree and slowly takes its place. The technique is named after it.

items: Don't try to move every path at once. One path, one week, one result.
Forget to delete the old code and both systems keep running forever.

check.q: Why is the strangler fig lower-risk than rewriting the whole app?
check.a: Only one small path moves at a time, and if there's trouble you go back with one line in the router. The whole system never changes in one day, and users notice nothing.

slides.title: Two apps, one database, one login
slides.tldr: While both apps run they share the database and the login cookie. Change shared data by adding before removing, and let the new app ask the old one who is logged in.

blocks.body: While both apps run, they share two things. **The database**: both read and write the same tables, so renaming a column for the new app breaks the old one at once. **The login**: the browser holds one session cookie, but each app keeps its own sessions, so a user logged in on the old app looks like a stranger to the new one.

blocks.code:
-- The new app wants integer cents, so rename the column
ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN total TO total_cents;

-- The old app, still running, now fails on every order page:
-- SELECT total FROM orders  ->  ERROR: unknown column 'total'

marks.tip: The old app still asks for `total`, so every page that shows an order breaks the moment this runs.
Adding a nullable column breaks nobody, because the old app never selects it.
Old rows get their cents value, so the new app can read every order.
The drop is the one step you can't take back. It waits until no old code reads `total`.

blocks.caption: Sharing the login while both apps run

steps.title: 1. One address
steps.body: The router serves both apps on one domain, so the browser sends the same cookie to both.
steps.tip: Cookies belong to a domain, not to an app. One domain in front means no extra login for the user.

steps.title: 2. Ask the old app
steps.body: The new app sends the cookie to a private /internal/whoami on the old app and gets back the user id.
steps.tip: The old app is still the one that knows its sessions. Asking it avoids copying session data between the two.

steps.title: 3. Keep it private
steps.body: That endpoint must be reachable only from inside your network, never from the internet.
steps.tip: Anyone who can call it with a stolen cookie learns who it belongs to, so it must not face the internet.

steps.title: 4. Move login last
steps.body: When /login itself moves to the new app, delete the whoami call.
steps.tip: Once the new app creates the sessions itself, it no longer needs to ask.

blocks.body: While both apps run, change shared data only by adding. Remove only after the old app is gone.

items.meaning: A small token the browser sends with every request so the server knows which logged-in user it is.
Changing a shared table in two safe phases: first add the new thing, and remove the old thing only much later.

items: The whoami call is an extra network hop on every request. Cache the answer for a short time, or the old app becomes the bottleneck.

check.q: Why not just rename the `total` column while the old app is still running?
check.a: The old app still selects `total`, so it breaks at once. Add the new column first, backfill it, switch the new app over, and drop the old column only after the old app is gone.

slides.title: Anti-corruption layer: keep the old system's odd language out
slides.tldr: Don't let the legacy system's odd names and formats into new code; confine them to one translator class.

blocks.body: The old system returns `st = 'A'`, `nm`, and money as the string "1250.50". If that language spreads into the new code, the new code becomes as messy as the old. The fix is a translator in the middle: the new code speaks its own clean language, and the translator converts the old system's language for it.

blocks.caption: The translator class turns the old language into the new one

nodes.label: New code
nodes.tip: The new code uses clean names and types. It doesn't recognize any of the old names.

nodes.label: Anti-corruption layer
nodes.tip: The only place where the old system's odd names are understood. If the old system changes, only this needs touching.

nodes.label: Legacy system
nodes.tip: The old system with its odd names and formats. None of it will leak into new code.

edges.label: The new code asks for a customer through a clean interface
The translator sends the request in the old language
The answer comes back in the old format
The translator returns a clean Customer object

marks.tip: Every place that reads the old row must know that "A" means active. Rename it once and you hunt through all of them.
The balance is still the string "1250.50", so this is float arithmetic on money.
The old `st` value becomes the new code's `active` bool. This translation happens only here.
The decimal amount becomes integer cents, because the new code doesn't use floats for money.

blocks.body: Don't let the old system's language into new code; translate it at the border.

use: You will talk to the old system for months or years.
Its names or formats are odd, or likely to change.
avoid: A throwaway one-time import: convert in the script and be done.
The price: one more class to write and keep in step with the old system.

items.label: Staying in sync with outside systems

check.q: If the old system renames the `st` field, where does code have to change, given an ACL?
check.a: Only in LegacyCustomerGateway. The rest of the new code knows `Customer::active`, not the old field name, so it never notices.

slides.title: Add a second server and users get logged out
slides.tldr: If sessions and uploaded files live on one server's disk, adding a second server means users are logged in one minute and logged out the next.

blocks.body: Ryan's app ran happily on one server. When traffic grew, he added a second server behind a load balancer. Soon the complaints started: "Sometimes I'm logged in, sometimes I'm not," and "I uploaded a photo and now it's gone." The reason: the session files and uploaded photos lived only on the first server's disk.

blocks.caption: Log in on one server, send the next request to another

actors.label: User
actors.tip: Sends two requests from the same browser, but the load balancer routes them to different servers.

actors.label: Server A
actors.tip: The login session file was created on its disk.

actors.label: Server B
actors.tip: It has no copy of that session file, so it has no idea who this user is.

messages.label: Wants to see their profile
messages.tip: This time the load balancer picked the other server.

blocks.body: A server must never remember anything about a user on its own.

aside.title: The owner who kept the tab in his head
aside.body: If the coffee shop owner keeps everyone's tab only in his head, it all vanishes the day he takes a vacation, and the assistant behind the counter can't tell anyone what they owe. Write it in a ledger and whoever sits at the counter sees the right numbers.

check.q: Why do users lose their login after a second server is added?
check.a: The session file sits on one server's disk. When the load balancer sends a request to the other server, it doesn't recognize the user.

slides.title: Stateless means: memory lives outside the server
slides.tldr: A stateless server remembers nothing itself, so any server can handle any request; the memory lives in the database, Redis or object storage.

blocks.title: The credit ledger on the counter
blocks.body: Picture a shop with three counters and three clerks, none of whom remembers a customer's name or what they owe. Everything is written in one central ledger, and whoever is on duty opens it and looks. So any counter can serve any customer, and adding a fourth counter on a busy day is easy.

blocks.caption: Where things on a server's disk should move

rows.tip: Every server reads sessions from the same Redis, so logins survive no matter which server gets the request.
Files go to shared storage, not a server disk. They survive even when a server dies.
A cache in each server's own memory shows different values on different servers. A shared cache gives everyone the same answer.
Two separate locks on two servers means no lock at all. The lock has to live in one place that everyone shares.
If the program writes logs to stdout, the platform can collect them all in one place.

blocks.title: What you gain
items: Any server can handle any request, so adding servers adds capacity.
When a server dies no data is lost, and a fresh one picks up the work immediately.
You can replace servers one by one while deploying new code.

items.meaning: The load balancer always sends the same user to the same server. Not a fix, just a hidden weakness.
A separate service for storing files (S3, MinIO), where files are saved and fetched by key.

check.q: Why are sticky sessions a poor fix for the login problem?
check.a: If that server dies or is replaced during a deploy, its users lose their sessions, and load is spread unevenly. The real fix is moving sessions out of the server.

slides.title: Two steps to make Symfony stateless
slides.tldr: Send sessions to Redis with one line of config, and write uploads through a Flysystem storage instead of the local disk. The storage config is on the next slide.

blocks.code:
framework:
    session:
        # every server keeps its sessions in the same Redis
        handler_id: '%env(REDIS_URL)%'
        cookie_secure: auto
        cookie_samesite: lax

marks.tip: Give Symfony a Redis DSN and it writes sessions there. No code changes, just config.
The storage named `$uploadsStorage` is autowired. Whether it is S3 or local is decided in config (next slide).
Keep only the file's key in the database, not the file itself. You can build the URL later.

items: In local development use the local adapter with the same code; in production use S3. Only config changes.
Temporary working files (building a zip) can use the local disk, as long as they finish within the same request.

check.q: Why store only a key in the database instead of the uploaded file itself?
check.a: The file lives in object storage that every server can reach, and the database holds just a small key. That keeps the database light, and you can switch storage without touching the code.

slides.title: Point the storage name at S3 (and at disk in dev)
slides.tldr: One Flysystem config says what stands behind the storage name: S3 in production, a local folder in dev. The upload code never changes.

blocks.body: On the last slide, `$uploadsStorage` was only a name. This file decides what stands behind it. Without it the upload lands on Server A's disk, and a request that reaches Server B gets a 404 for the photo. The price: every file read or write is now a network call, slower than a local disk, and you pay S3 per gigabyte and per request.

blocks.code:
when@prod:
    flysystem:
        storages:
            uploads.storage:
                adapter: 'aws'
                options:
                    client: 'Aws\S3\S3Client'
                    bucket: '%env(UPLOADS_BUCKET)%'

when@dev:
    flysystem:
        storages:
            uploads.storage:
                adapter: 'local'
                options:
                    directory: '%kernel.project_dir%/var/uploads'

marks.tip: The storage name `uploads.storage` becomes the autowired argument `FilesystemOperator $uploadsStorage`.
The S3 adapter. All servers write to and read from the same bucket.
In dev the same name points at a folder, so nobody needs an S3 account to work on the app.

blocks.code:
services:
    Aws\S3\S3Client:
        arguments:
            - version: 'latest'
              region: '%env(AWS_REGION)%'
              # no keys here: on AWS the server's IAM role supplies them

marks.tip: The service id the Flysystem `client:` option refers to. Symfony builds it once and shares it.

use: Anything users upload or download that must survive a server dying.
avoid: Temporary files that live and die inside one request. The local disk is faster.

items: Add a `when@test:` block with the local adapter so tests never touch S3.

check.q: What breaks if flysystem.yaml is missing and the code still writes to $uploadsStorage?
check.a: Symfony cannot autowire the storage at all. If you point it at a local folder instead, each server keeps its own files and the other server returns a 404.

slides.title: Serverless: like a taxi, you pay per ride
slides.tldr: With serverless the platform runs the servers and you pay for what you use; in return you accept cold starts and limits.

blocks.title: Your own car vs a ride-share
blocks.body: If you own a car, you pay for the driver, fuel and garage whether you drive or not. With a ride-share you pay only for the trips you take, but after you call, the car takes a while to arrive. Serverless works the same way: your code runs when a request arrives and costs almost nothing when none does. That wait for the car is the cold start.

blocks.caption: The first request after a long quiet spell: a cold start

actors.label: User
actors.tip: Sends the request. The first one waits longer, later ones don't.

actors.label: Platform
actors.tip: A service like Lambda or Cloud Run that creates and shuts down places to run your code.

actors.label: Your code
actors.tip: Your function or Symfony app, running inside a container.

messages.label: Start a new instance (cold start)
messages.tip: Downloading the code and booting the runtime and framework. This is the delay.

messages.label: Next request: instance is warm, fast

blocks.title: Three facts to remember
items: Your code must be stateless, because an instance can be stopped or recreated at any moment.
Every call has a time limit (for example, 15 minutes at most on Lambda).
When many instances run at once, the number of database connections jumps with them.

blocks.body: That last fact bites first. 1,000 visitors at once means about 1,000 instances, each opening its own database connection. A small MySQL server accepts about 150 by default, so the rest are refused. The fix is a connection pooler or proxy (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer): instances talk to it, and it lends out, say, 50 real connections between them. Its price is one more moving part to run.

items: You can run a PHP/Symfony app on AWS Lambda with Bref. Services like Cloud Run run ordinary containers.

check.q: What is a cold start in serverless, and when does it hurt most?
check.a: It is the wait for a new instance to start on the first request after a quiet period. It hurts most when every response must be very fast and traffic is spiky.

slides.title: When serverless fits, and when it doesn't
slides.tldr: For bursty or irregular work serverless is cheap and easy; for heavy, constant or long-running work your own servers or containers are better.

columns.title: Fits

A report or cron job that runs once a night
Handling webhooks with irregular traffic
Prototypes with new, unknown traffic

Does the job finish within the time limit, and can you live with the cold start delay?
Is your team willing to learn the platform's limits and its new way of logging and debugging?

slides.title: "Fast, always up, secure, and cheap, please"
slides.tldr: Asking for the maximum of everything isn't a requirement, it's a decision avoided; and vague wishes can't be measured, so nobody knows when the work is done.

blocks.body: An e-commerce client told Ryan's team, "The app has to be fast, always up, as secure as possible, cheap to run and easy to change." The team said, "Sure." Six months later the site crawled on sale day, and the client said, "I told you it had to be fast!" The team replied, "Nobody said how fast." A wish becomes a requirement only when it carries a number, such as "checkout answers in under 300ms when 100 people pay at once."

blocks.caption: What the client asked for, and the questions nobody could answer

columns.title: What was asked
items: Fast
Always up
Completely secure
Cheap
Easy to change
columns.tip: All five were requested at "the best". In practice they pull against each other.

columns.title: Questions with no answer
items: How fast: 200ms or 2 seconds?
How available: 99% or 99.99%?
What budget, how many dollars a month?
How many people arrive at once, and when?
columns.tip: Behind every wish hides a number that nobody asked for.

aside.body: A vague wish can't be measured, and if you can't measure it you can't say whether the work is finished. So the argument happens after the release, when changing things costs the most.

items.meaning: Not what the system does but how well it does it: speed, uptime, security and so on.
Non-functional requirement: another name for a quality attribute.

check.q: What mistake did Ryan's team make when the client said "it has to be fast"?
check.a: They never asked "how fast, and under what conditions?" Without a number, "fast" can't be measured, so nobody knows when the goal has been met.

slides.title: Five qualities, and each one is paid for by another
slides.tldr: Speed, availability, security, maintainability and cost can't all be maxed out together; raising one lowers another.

blocks.title: The bus ticket: fast, comfortable, cheap
blocks.body: Traveling from New York to Boston, you can't have fast, comfortable and cheap all at once. A first-class train seat is comfortable but pricey, and a local bus is cheap but slow. Software is the same: every quality has a price, and you pay it out of another quality.

blocks.caption: Raise one quality and something else gives
headers: What you do to raise it

rows.tip: A cache is a stored answer. It can go stale, and keeping it clean is a whole new job.
To survive a failure you must keep spares of everything, and every spare brings its own problems.
Each extra guard is an extra step for the user or extra work for the database.
You can skip it in today's rush. But every later feature pays interest on that choice.
Saving money usually means fewer resources, which can mean less speed or less security.

blocks.body: No system maxes out every quality. Deciding what to pay for what is the architecture decision.

aside.body: Every time, ask: "To raise this quality, which other quality am I giving up?"

check.q: You run two servers to raise availability. What does it cost you in the other qualities?
check.a: Cost roughly doubles and complexity grows: a load balancer, data syncing, and keeping the two servers consistent. In return the system stays up when one of them dies.

slides.title: Turn vague wishes into numbers
slides.tldr: Write each quality as a scenario, a measure and a target, and everyone can tell whether the work is done.

blocks.body: Here's a template that makes a vague word measurable: in what situation, what do we measure, and what value counts as good. "Fast" becomes "when 100 people check out at once during a sale, p95 latency stays under 300ms." p95 means 95 out of 100 requests are faster than that figure. The same target is later checked by tests and monitoring.

blocks.caption: From vague wish to measurable target

rows.tip: It has a situation, a measure and a number. Now a load test can actually verify it.

cells: Monthly uptime >= 99.9% (no more than about 43 minutes down a month)
rows.tip: 99.9% allows roughly 43 minutes of downtime a month. Knowing that number lets you work out the cost.

cells: Login locked 15 minutes after 5 wrong passwords; critical CVEs fixed in 7 days
rows.tip: A few specific, checkable rules. A CVE is a publicly listed security hole in some software. Saying "completely secure" says nothing.
With a budget ceiling, you choose the other qualities inside that limit.

cells: Adding a new payment gateway takes <= 3 days
rows.tip: The test: time how long this change really takes. If it takes longer, the structure is wrong.

- id: QA-1
  attribute: performance
  scenario: 'When 100 people press checkout at once during a sale'
  measure: 'p95 latency of the checkout API'
  target: '< 300ms'
  verify: 'k6 load test, in CI before every release'

- id: QA-2
  attribute: availability
  scenario: 'When one app server dies'
  measure: 'monthly uptime'
  target: '>= 99.9%'
  verify: 'health check + external uptime monitor'

marks.tip: Without a verify line the target is only on paper. Write down how it will be checked, too.

items.desc: run a load test and get the p95

check.q: Which three things do you add to "the system should be fast" to make it measurable?
check.a: A scenario (how many users, when), a measure (such as p95 latency) and a target value (such as under 300ms).

slides.title: Pick the top two first, then put limits on the rest
slides.tldr: For each system pick the two most important qualities, set a minimum bar for the others, and keep the price of each extra "nine" in mind.

blocks.body: You can't give every quality equal weight. In a payments app like PayPal, security and availability come first and cost comes last. On a personal blog, cost and maintainability come first and availability comes last. Write the decision down, because six months from now someone will ask, "Why didn't we go for 99.99%?" Below is what that record looks like for a shop's checkout.

blocks.caption: Four steps to prioritize qualities

steps.title: 1. List all five
steps.body: Speed, availability, security, maintainability, cost.
steps.tip: With all five in front of you, you notice the one you were forgetting.

steps.title: 2. Pick two
steps.body: Which two hurt the business most if they break?
steps.tip: Think in terms of damage: which failure would wreck the business or its users' trust?

steps.title: 3. Bound the rest
steps.body: Set a minimum measurable bar for each of them.
steps.tip: The others aren't dropped, just lower priority. They still must not fall below a bar.

steps.title: 4. Write it down
steps.body: Record the decision and why in an ADR.
steps.tip: A short ADR is enough. If you skip the reason, the same argument returns later.

A reasonable target for most business systems. It needs a standby server that is ready to go.
No time for a human to step in, so recovery must be fully automatic. Cost climbs sharply.
Overkill almost everywhere. Unless it's something like banking or telecom, it isn't worth the price.

The one business number the decision rests on. Ask the users what an hour of downtime costs.

Revisit the priorities every few months; when the business changes, the targets change.

check.q: Why is 99.999% availability not always a good goal?
check.a: Each extra nine multiplies the cost, and most businesses don't need it. If it costs more than the downtime would, it's wasted money.

slides.title: How much rice for a 500-guest wedding?
slides.tldr: You don't need an exact answer; two minutes of rough math on a scrap of paper catches a 10x mistake, and that is enough to decide.

blocks.body: The client asked Ryan, "A million users are coming. How many servers do we need?" Ryan guessed "50." Someone else said "just one." Neither had done any math. Five minutes with pen and paper would have shown that both were wrong.

blocks.title: The wedding cook's rice sum
blocks.body: For a 500-guest wedding the cook writes: 500 guests x 0.5 lb each = 250 lb, plus 25 lb extra. It isn't exact, but it stops him buying 25 lb or 2,500 lb. Estimating system capacity works the same way: round the numbers, multiply them, and catch the 10x mistake.

blocks.caption: Deciding by guesswork vs a sum on paper

columns.title: Deciding by guess
items: Saying "50 servers" wastes money
Saying "one is enough" takes the site down on sale day
Nobody knows where the number came from
columns.tip: A number with no calculation behind it is a stone thrown in the dark. It could be 10x too high or 10x too low.

columns.title: A sum on paper
items: Step-by-step multiplication and division, every assumption written down
Answer: about 3, not 50 and not 1
Change any assumption and the sum is easy to redo
columns.tip: Five minutes of rough math tells you how many servers you need, and which assumption would change the answer.

aside.body: Before you decide what the system looks like, you must know whether the number is 10, 10 thousand or 10 million. An estimate gives you that order of magnitude.

items.meaning: Queries (requests) per second: how many requests arrive each second.
Daily active users: how many people actually use the app on a given day.

check.q: Why is an estimate useful even when it isn't exact?
check.a: Its job is to catch 10x mistakes: to tell whether you need 1 server, 10 or 100. You can measure the exact figure later.

slides.title: From users to servers: a chain of multiplications
slides.tldr: Multiply users by requests each, divide by 86,400 to get QPS, apply a peak factor, then divide by what one server can handle.

nodes.label: 1M DAU
nodes.tip: The starting assumption. Not total users, but how many actually open the app on a given day.

nodes.label: 5M/day
nodes.tip: Assuming each person checks tracking 5 times a day: 1 million times 5.

nodes.label: ≈ 60 QPS
nodes.tip: 5 million divided by 86,400 seconds is about 58. Rounded to 60.

nodes.label: ≈ 300 QPS
nodes.tip: 5 times the average. You build servers for the busy hour, not for the average.

nodes.label: 3 servers
nodes.tip: 300 divided by 150 (the assumed capacity of one server) is 2, plus one spare in case one dies.

edges.label: At 5 requests per person per day, that makes 5 million
Divide by the 86,400 seconds in a day to get the average QPS
Multiply the average by 5 to cover the busy hour
Divide by one server's capacity, then add a spare

blocks.body: Picture 300 QPS as 300 people pressing "track my parcel" in the very same second, like a full cricket stadium all knocking at once. If one server can answer about 150 of them per second (an assumed figure, you would measure it), you need 2, plus a spare.

requests/day = DAU x requests per user
QPS (avg)    = requests/day / 86,400       (quick: / 100,000)
QPS (peak)   = avg x 3 to 10               (usually 5)
servers      = peak / one server's capacity + 1 spare

marks.tip: Dividing by 100,000 is easy and only about 15% off. That is good enough for an estimate.
The factor depends on the business. On sale days or match nights it can reach 10, so check your own history.

blocks.body: Round your numbers. Catching a 10x error matters; a 10% error does not.

To find your peak factor, look in the access log at the busiest hour's requests.

check.q: If 8.6 million requests arrive per day, what is the average QPS, and why is it wrong to size servers on it?
check.a: About 100 QPS. But the busy hour brings several times that, so you size servers for peak QPS, not the average.

check.a: About 120. 1 million requests/day is roughly 12 QPS, so 10 million is 10 times that, around 120.

slides.tldr: For one app: QPS, servers, storage, bandwidth, memory and cost on one sheet. The answer is modest: about 3 servers, not 50 and not 1.

check.a: Don't worry about the network. Spend your time on the number of servers and the database, which are this app's real limits.

slides.title: Four traps in estimation
slides.tldr: Forgetting peak load, forgetting replicas and indexes, treating assumptions as facts, and showing false precision are what ruin estimates.

blocks.caption: The bad habits and their fixes

columns.title: Bad habit
items: Using only average QPS, ignoring peak
Forgetting indexes and replicas in storage
Presenting an estimate as an exact fact
Writing "57.3 servers"
columns.tip: These four mistakes either make the numbers look too small or create blind trust.

columns.title: Good habit
items: Average x peak factor, with the source of the factor noted
Storage x 2-3 for indexes and replicas
Writing down each assumption separately
"About 3", a rounded answer
columns.tip: The opposite habit blocks each trap.

blocks.body: See two traps on the package delivery app. Average only: 60 QPS looks like one 150-QPS server is plenty, but the busy hour brings 300, twice what it can do, so replies crawl or time out. Raw storage only: 120 GB fits a 200 GB disk, but with indexes and a replica you need 240-360 GB, and the disk is full before the year ends.

blocks.title: Three things to do after the sum
items: List the assumptions and mark the one that changes the answer the most.
Measure that one first: run a load test or open the access log.
Give a range: "2 to 5 servers". It is more honest than a single number.

blocks.body: An estimate gives the scale of a question, not the answer. When it turns out wrong, change the numbers, not the method.

items: If you have real data, use it instead of guessing. Estimate only where you have no data.
Write the assumptions down. Otherwise in six months nobody knows what the system was built on.

items.label: Checking assumptions in a design review

check.q: Which two habits make an estimate most trustworthy?
check.a: Writing down each assumption separately, and measuring first whichever one changes the answer most. And give the result as a range.

slides.title: Five hundred users, six technologies
slides.tldr: Every new technology brings the cost of running it for life, not just of installing it, and a small team sinks under that weight.

blocks.title: New machines at the pizza place
blocks.body: Kevin's pizza place has two ovens and three staff. After visiting a big restaurant, he buys a wood-fired oven, an espresso machine and a gelato machine. Now each machine needs its own repairman, its own spare parts and its own training. In the Friday dinner rush the wood-fired oven breaks down, and nobody in the restaurant knows how to fix it.
A team of three does exactly this when it puts MongoDB, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Kubernetes under an app with 500 users, thinking "that's what the big companies run."

blocks.caption: The same app with two different stacks: which one costs more sleep?

columns.title: What would have worked fine
items: Symfony: a single app
PostgreSQL: data, search and queue in one
One server, a simple deploy
columns.tip: Two familiar technologies. All three people know both well, so anyone can fix any problem.

columns.title: What got installed
items: Symfony + PostgreSQL (as before)
MongoDB: because someone said "fast"
Kafka: because "we'll need to scale later"
Elasticsearch: for search
Kubernetes: to run all of the above
columns.tip: Six technologies, three people. Each needs its own deploy, backup, monitoring and upgrades, and nobody knows them all deeply.

aside.title: The 3 a.m. phone call
aside.body: At one startup, the person who had set up Kafka quit. Three months later one night messages got stuck and orders started piling up. The other two spent the whole night reading documentation, because the technology wasn't known by the team. It was known by one person.

items.meaning: All the technologies it takes to run an app, taken together.
Building a bigger, more complex solution than the problem needs.
