A document database, a high-volume message pipeline, a search engine, and a manager for fleets of containers. All real tools, built for loads far bigger than 500 users.

check.q: Even when a technology is free, where does it still cost the team?
check.a: In learning, deploying, monitoring, backups, upgrades and fixing it when it breaks. Each takes team time, and the bill keeps coming for as long as the technology stays.

slides.title: The complexity budget and boring technology
slides.tldr: A team's attention is a limited budget: spend it on new technology only where it moves the business forward, and use familiar tools everywhere else.

blocks.body: Just as the restaurant's three staff can learn to run only a few machines well, a team can know only a few technologies deeply. That limit is the **complexity budget**: the amount of complexity you can afford to spend. Every new database, queue or language draws from it. **Boring technology** doesn't mean old or weak. It means technology whose ways of breaking are already well known to everyone.

blocks.caption: Five costs that come with every new technology

rows.tip: One person knowing it isn't enough. When they go on holiday or quit, the rest are helpless, so everyone has to learn.
Every technology needs its own dashboard, its own backup method and its own alerts, built and watched.
Postpone upgrades and you leave security holes; do them and something may break. Both take time.
A familiar technology's error is one search away from a fix. With an unfamiliar one, the same problem eats the whole night.

cells: Moving the data to something else
rows.tip: Easy to put in, hard to take out. Once the data piles up, dropping a technology becomes a project of its own.

blocks.title: Rules for spending the budget
items: Ask first: can what we already have do the job? If yes, add nothing new.
Only one unfamiliar technology at a time; the next one only after the team knows the last.
Adopt new technology only where it puts the business ahead of its competitors.

blocks.body: Buying a new technology is a one-time cost. Running it is a lifetime one.

aside.title: Three innovation tokens
aside.body: In his well-known essay "Choose Boring Technology", Dan McKinley suggests that every company has only about three "innovation tokens". An unfamiliar database spends one, an unfamiliar language spends another. So spend your tokens carefully, where the payoff is greatest.
Boring doesn't mean bad. Boring means no surprises, and in production no surprises is what you want.

use: A measured need your current tools cannot meet, for example search that is still too slow after tuning.
A feature that sets the business apart and truly needs the new tool.
avoid: "Big companies use it" or "we'll need it later" with no number behind it.
A second unfamiliar technology while the first is still new to the team.

check.q: What does "boring technology" really mean?
check.a: Not old or weak technology, but technology whose failure modes are well known from years of use. So there are fewer surprises, and fixes are easy to find.

slides.title: Three roads: build, buy, open source
slides.tldr: Build what sets your business apart, buy what everyone needs in the same way, and take open source when you can run a mature tool.

blocks.title: Three ways to get the restaurant's tiramisu
blocks.body: Kevin can **make** tiramisu (a layered coffee dessert) from his own recipe: the taste is entirely his, but it takes a month of testing and cooking every day. He can **buy** it every day from a bakery: it's available from tomorrow, but the price and taste are in the shop's hands. Or he can use a **free recipe** published by a famous chef: the recipe costs nothing, but shopping, cooking and any spoiled batch are on him. Open source is that third option.

blocks.caption: What you get and what you give on each road

rows.tip: Buying gets you started fastest. If you build, you don't get any benefit from day one.
No road is free. The cost just lands in different places: sometimes the bill, sometimes people's time.

cells: As much as the vendor allows
Code is open, you can change it
rows.tip: With something you bought, a new feature means waiting for the vendor. With your own or open code you can change it yourself.

cells: Takes long, every bug is yours
Lacking the skills to run it
rows.tip: Each road has a different risk. Before deciding, ask: can my team handle this one?

cells: Tool is mature, you can run it
rows.tip: For example: build your own pricing rules; buy payments, SMS and email; take a framework and database as open source.

blocks.body: Build what sets you apart from competitors. For what everyone needs in the same way, buy or use something ready-made.

items.meaning: A service that runs on someone else's servers and is used for a monthly fee. You run nothing yourself.
The part of the business that customers come to you for.
Insisting on building it yourself even when a good solution already exists.

items: Building your own login, payments or encryption: a small mistake there is very costly, and tested solutions are right at hand.
Putting production on one person's hobby open source project.

check.q: For a food delivery app, which should you build and which buy: the rider assignment rules, or sending SMS?
check.a: Build the rider assignment rules, because that's what sets the business apart. Sending SMS is the same for everyone, so buy it.

slides.title: TCO: working out the real three-year price
slides.tldr: The price isn't just the license or the monthly bill: setup + running + people's time + exit cost. Compare three-year totals.

blocks.body: **TCO** (total cost of ownership) is the total cost of a thing over the whole time you keep it. The biggest and best-hidden item in it is engineer time. Below is a calculation for adding product search to a shop app: **build** = write it yourself on PostgreSQL full-text search, **buy** = a SaaS search service, **open source** = OpenSearch on your own server. We assume one engineer-day costs $500.

blocks.caption: Product search: three-year cost in thousands of dollars (assumed figures for the example)

rows.tip: Engineer-days x $500. If you buy, you only plug in an API, so the start is cheapest.
OpenSearch is free to license but needs its own server, assumed at $700 a month. The SaaS bill is $1,200 a month.
Upgrades, backups, monitoring, fixing problems: days per month x $500 x 36. This is the line everyone forgets.
In this example the "free" open source option is the most expensive, because it needs both a server and running time. Your numbers may give a different result.

cells: 5 days: swap our own search code
rows.tip: Days it would take to drop this option later, at $500 a day. Kept out of the total because you may never pay it, but it is the price of changing your mind.

blocks.caption: The three-year totals side by side

items.label: Build
items.tip: 30 days of work upfront, but no new server and no bill. Richer features would still cost more time later.

items.label: Buy
items.tip: Most of the cost is the monthly bill. If usage grew tenfold and the bill with it, that is 12 x 36 = 432 thousand, and building would win easily. Work that out separately.

items.label: Open source
items.tip: The license costs nothing, yet the total is highest: $25,200 on the server and $54,000 on running it.

blocks.title: The four steps of the calculation
items: Initial cost: engineer-days to build or set up x the cost of one day.
Running cost: monthly bill or server + maintenance days per month, over 36 months.
Exit cost: also write down how many days it would take to drop this tomorrow.
Add it up and compare, then decide with risk and your team's skills in mind.
Counting engineer time as zero: the most common mistake.
Looking only at the first month's bill and not at what it will be if usage grows tenfold.
When the numbers are about equal, picking the shiny new option over the familiar one.

aside.body: Price = setup + running + exit. The license is only one line of it.

check.q: If an open source tool's license is free, which costs still remain in its TCO?
check.a: Setup and learning time, the server bill, the monthly time for upgrades, backups and monitoring, and the cost of moving to something else later.

slides.title: You bought it, but left no exit door
slides.tldr: If a vendor's SDK spreads across your code, switching vendors is nearly impossible; behind an interface, the change happens in one place.

blocks.body: Buying isn't the mistake. Letting the vendor into every corner of your code is. If the bakery's name were printed on all of Kevin's menus, bills and signboards, he couldn't leave even when the shop doubled its prices. In software this is called **vendor lock-in**. In the code below, the SMS vendor's class sits right inside business code.

marks.tip: The vendor's name is inside business code. To switch vendors, each of these 40 places must be rewritten and retested.
Even the way you call it is vendor-specific. Another vendor's SDK will name its methods and options differently.
The code knows only an interface. Which vendor sends the SMS is decided by a DSN in config, and this class never knows.
To switch vendors you change the DSN, the matching line in notifier.yaml and one composer package; this line stays exactly as it is.

blocks.body: Only one place should know the vendor. Everything else knows only the interface.

aside.title: The whole job of switching vendors

items.desc: Install the Notifier bridge for the vendor you want
The DSN in .env.local; the vendor's name lives only here
The one matching line in config/packages/notifier.yaml

items: If Symfony has no bridge for your vendor, write a small interface of your own and keep all the vendor's code in a single adapter class.
Before signing, ask: in what format can I get my data out, and how easily?
The price of the interface: you can only use what every vendor offers. Skip it for tools you will never swap.

items.label: Keeping vendors apart with ports and adapters

check.q: In a good design, how many places do you touch to change SMS vendors, and why?
check.a: One: the config or a single adapter class. The rest of the code knows only the interface and never learns the vendor's name.

slides.title: Two teams, two stacks, two kinds of pain
slides.tldr: Both teams picked a stack by fashion or habit instead of by the job, and each paid for it in the part of the system that mattered most.

blocks.title: Choosing a vehicle for the route
blocks.body: A delivery company owner in Dallas buys the same vehicle his neighbor just bought. A cargo van is perfect for a narrow alley downtown, but it can't haul ten tons of produce to Houston. A semi truck can, but it won't fit down the alley.

Neither vehicle is bad. The load and the road decide. Ryan's team is building a policy and claims system for an insurance company, and Nicole's team is building a video-streaming site. Both picked a stack the way the owner picked his vehicle.

blocks.caption: Same mistake, different pain: the stack was chosen before the job was understood

columns.title: Ryan: insurance, chosen by fashion
items: Picked a trendy, minimal toolkit after a conference talk
Nothing built in for roles, audit trail or nightly batch jobs
Premiums kept as floating-point numbers; totals drifted by a few cents
Months spent hand-building what other stacks ship ready and tested
columns.tip: A trendy minimal toolkit looked fast in a conference talk. But an insurance system lives on money rules, permissions and records, and the toolkit left all of that to the team.

columns.title: Nicole: video, chosen by habit
items: Picked the stack the team already knew from a bank project
Converted uploads inside the web request, so the site froze
Streamed every video straight from the app server; lag and bills grew
The web framework was never the bottleneck
columns.tip: The team knew this stack from a bank project, so they never asked where a video site spends its effort. The real work is converting and delivering big files, not rendering pages.

aside.title: The cent that did not add up
aside.body: At month-end the auditors found that the premium report was a few dollars away from the sum of the individual policies. Money had been stored as floating-point numbers, which can't hold a value like 0.1 exactly, and rounded in different places. With no audit trail, nobody could prove which figure was right.

items.meaning: The language, framework, database and supporting tools you build an application on.
A record of who changed what and when, kept so a change can be traced later.
Converting an uploaded video into several sizes and formats so any phone or screen can play it.

check.q: Neither stack was bad. So why did both teams end up in trouble?
check.a: Each chose by fashion or habit before asking what the job needed. The insurance team had no built-in safety for money and audit; the video team put the heavy work in the wrong place.

slides.title: Start from the job: six questions
slides.tldr: Write down what the application needs first (workload, correctness, built-ins, integrations, people, support), then see which stack fits, not the other way around.

blocks.body: The transport owner asks what he carries, on which road, and who will drive. A stack decision has the same questions. Answer them before you look at any framework, and the shortlist nearly writes itself.

blocks.caption: Six vehicle questions, six stack questions

cells: Video bytes, or many small money transactions
rows.tip: What the system spends its time on: moving big files, waiting on other services, applying many rules, or recording many small changes safely.

cells: Exact decimals, strict transactions, audit trail
rows.tip: For money and legal records a wrong value is a real loss. For a video thumbnail it is not. The more fragile the cargo, the more you want proven built-in protection.

cells: Transactions, security, batch jobs, scheduling, ORM
rows.tip: Each feature the framework already ships is one you do not write, test, patch or explain to every new hire.
A stack that talks easily to your existing systems saves more than a faster one that needs glue code everywhere.

cells: Who can drive and repair it?
Skills you have, people you can hire
rows.tip: A great stack that nobody on the team knows is a risk. Also ask who you can hire in your city when someone leaves.

cells: How long are spare parts made?
rows.tip: An application may live ten years. Check how long a version gets security fixes and how painful upgrades usually are.

blocks.body: Let the job choose the stack. Never let the stack choose the job.

items.meaning: What the system mostly does: move big files, wait on other services, crunch numbers, or record many small changes safely.
How well known the ways to deploy, monitor, back up and repair it are.

use: The job has clear needs, such as money, audit or heavy media, that a stack either serves well or does not.
avoid: The needs are ordinary CRUD and your team already knows a mature stack. Then the team's skill decides, and you can stop here.

check.q: Name three things about the job you should settle before shortlisting any framework.
check.a: For example: the workload shape, how strict the correctness needs are (money, audit), and what the framework already provides. Integration, team skills and support length are the other three.

slides.title: Worked example: a video site and an insurance system
slides.tldr: Ask the same six questions of both jobs. The answers differ, so what you look for in a stack differs, and several stacks can still fit either job.

blocks.body: Here are the six questions answered for both teams. Read each row across: the same question gets a different answer, and so a different shopping list.

blocks.caption: Same questions, two jobs, two shopping lists

cells: Big files, many viewers, a lot of I/O waiting
Many small writes, rules, reports, month-end batches
rows.tip: Video is mostly bytes moving. Insurance is mostly rules applied to records, safely, again and again.

cells: A dropped frame annoys, it does not cost money
A wrong cent or lost record becomes a legal problem
rows.tip: This row decides how much you value ready-made, long-tested protection for money and records.
List the features you would otherwise write by hand. Those are the ones to look for in the framework.
Video integrates with infrastructure tools. Insurance integrates with old systems and outside institutions.

cells: Any strong web team; most of the pipeline is tools
Engineers who know the rules and the legacy
rows.tip: For video the team can learn the pipeline tools. For insurance, years of knowledge of the business rules are the scarce part.

cells: Many languages work; invest in the pipeline
Mature transactions, security, typing, long support
rows.tip: The conclusion is not one winning stack. It is a list of properties, and several stacks may have them.

blocks.caption: Where the video work really happens: the web backend only hands files over

nodes.label: Creator
nodes.tip: The person who uploads a new video.

nodes.label: Web app
nodes.tip: The web backend. It accepts the upload and the logins, then hands the heavy work to other parts.

nodes.label: Object storage
nodes.tip: A service that stores big files cheaply: the originals and every converted version.

nodes.label: Converter
nodes.tip: A background worker that converts each video into several sizes. This is where the real effort goes.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.tip: A content delivery network: servers around the world that keep copies of popular files close to viewers.

nodes.label: Viewer
nodes.tip: The person watching on a phone or laptop.

edges.label: The creator uploads a video and the web app accepts it.
The app saves the original in object storage and replies at once.
A background worker picks up the file and converts it into several sizes.
The converted versions are saved back to storage.
The CDN copies the popular files and keeps them near viewers.
Viewers stream from the CDN, not from the app server.

items: For a video site the budget goes into queues, storage, the CDN and the cost of delivery. The web layer can stay thin.
An insurance system is the reverse: the framework itself carries the rules, so its built-in features matter most.
Treating the two shopping lists as one verdict. The table says what to look for, not which brand to buy.

items.label: Quality attributes: what the system must be good at

check.q: Why does the web backend language matter less for the video site than for the insurance system?
check.a: The video site's heavy work (converting and delivering files) runs in storage, workers and a CDN, not in the web framework. The insurance system's core job, safe money rules, runs inside its framework.

slides.title: Built in, or build it yourself?
slides.tldr: Mature stacks ship transactions, security, batch and scheduling ready-made. Check what yours ships before you hand-build it, and know what that convenience costs.

blocks.body: A feature you don't write is a feature you don't test, patch or explain to every new hire. That's why Java with Spring Boot and C# with .NET are common in banks and insurers: they ship years-tested answers to the needs of money work. They aren't the only fit. Django can run accounting software, and so can Symfony, which this course uses.

blocks.caption: Three stacks and some of what each gives you built in

columns.title: Java + Spring Boot
items: Declarative transactions with @Transactional
Spring Security for login and permissions
Spring Batch for large, restartable jobs
Strong typing; long-term-support releases
columns.tip: A large, mature ecosystem used widely in enterprise systems. Strongly typed, with long-term-support Java releases.

columns.title: C# + .NET
items: Entity Framework Core: ORM and migrations
Dependency injection built into the platform
ASP.NET Core Identity for users and roles
Strong typing; long-term-support releases
columns.tip: Microsoft's stack, also common in enterprises. Strongly typed, with long-term-support releases and good tooling.

columns.title: PHP + Symfony
items: Doctrine ORM: transactions and migrations
Security voters for fine-grained permissions
Messenger for queues, Workflow for state rules
Lock and Scheduler for exclusivity and timed jobs
columns.tip: The stack of this course. It ships many of the same building blocks, so a CRUD developer can grow into money-heavy work without switching language.

blocks.body: Without these built-ins you write them: transaction handling, permission checks, a batch loop that can restart. Each is code you must test, and a bug in it touches money. The price of using them is learning the framework's way, more ceremony for small jobs, and a pull toward its ecosystem. All of it spends the [[thinking/build-vs-buy/too-many-machines|complexity budget]].

items.meaning: You mark a method, and the framework opens, commits or rolls back the database transaction for you.
A large job run on a schedule, such as month-end premiums, that must be able to resume after a failure.

use: Money, audit and long-lived rules dominate: favor mature built-ins, strong typing and long support.
Your team already masters a stack that meets the needs: use it.
avoid: Picking a stack only because a bank or a famous company uses it.
Ignoring who you can hire in your city when you choose.

check.q: Can Django run accounting software? Why do many insurers still pick Spring or .NET?
check.a: Yes, if you add and test what it lacks. Spring and .NET are common because transactions, security and batch ship built in, they are strongly typed, and their releases are supported for a long time.

slides.title: The trap: a fashionable rewrite or a benchmark winner
slides.tldr: Rewriting a working system into a trendy stack, or choosing by one speed benchmark, spends your complexity budget on a problem you never measured.

blocks.body: Kevin's old insurance system is slow at month-end. A new developer says, "Let's rewrite it in the stack from the benchmark charts." A year later the team runs two systems, the old rules are half re-created, and month-end is still slow. The cause was one missing database index.

blocks.caption: What the fashionable rewrite does, and what fixing the measured problem does

columns.title: Rewrite for fashion
items: Re-creates rules that took years to get right
Two systems run side by side for a long time
The team learns a new stack and ships nothing
The real cause, one slow query, is never measured
columns.tip: It feels bold, but it spends a huge amount of effort before it touches the real cause.

columns.title: Fix the measured problem
items: Measure first: find the slow query or step
Change the smallest part: add an index, queue the job
Keep the stack the team and the rules live in
Rewrite only when a measured limit has no other fix
columns.tip: It is small, quick to try and easy to undo, and it keeps the stack that your rules and people already live in.

blocks.title: Before you choose or change a stack
items: Write the needs down: workload, correctness, built-ins, integrations.
Check what the stack ships built in and how mature it is.
Count the team: skills today, hiring tomorrow, who is on call.
Check how long a version is supported and how upgrades go.
If the familiar option meets the needs, keep it. Spend budget only on a measured gap.

blocks.body: A benchmark answers one question. The stack decision asks six.

aside.title: Why rewrites run long
aside.body: Teams that rewrite a working system often find it takes far longer than planned. The old code holds years of small rules that nobody wrote down, and they only show up when the new system gets something wrong.

use: The stack has lost security support and cannot be upgraded.
A measured limit cannot be fixed inside the current stack.
avoid: Boredom, fashion, or one benchmark chart.

check.q: A month-end report is slow. What should you do before proposing a new stack?
check.a: Measure where the time goes and fix that part first. Change the stack only when a measured limit cannot be fixed inside the current one.

slides.title: One coupon feature, three teams' queues
slides.tldr: Work follows the way teams are split: with teams divided by layer, even a small feature waits in three queues.

blocks.body: A company has split its teams by layer: a UI team, a Backend team and a Database team. The "coupon code" feature needs just three changes: a form, an API and a table. But each change belongs to a different team, so the ticket finishes in one team's queue and then waits in the next. Two days of work takes three weeks. Put the same three people in one team that owns the form, the API and the table, and the ticket takes about its two days of real work: no handoff, no queue. The rest of this lesson shows how to get there.

blocks.caption: The coupon ticket passes through three teams' queues

nodes.label: Coupon ticket
nodes.tip: The business wants a discount when a coupon code is entered. It is really one piece of work.

nodes.label: UI team
nodes.tip: Sees only the frontend. Without the API, a finished form does nothing.

nodes.label: Backend team
nodes.tip: Sees only the API and business code. Without a column in the table, it is stuck.

nodes.label: Database team
nodes.tip: Schema and migrations are in this team's hands. They already have 12 other tickets in their own queue.

nodes.label: Live
nodes.tip: Two days of work, three weeks of waiting. The delay isn't in the code but in the handoffs.

edges.label: The ticket first joins the UI team's queue
The UI team builds the form, then files a ticket for the Backend team
The Backend team needs a column, so it files a ticket for the Database team
After three weeks in queues, the feature goes live

aside.title: Nobody made a mistake, yet it was late
aside.body: Every team did its own job properly and quickly. The delay came because each handoff means writing up a request, waiting, and fitting into another team's priorities. The problem wasn't the people, it was the way the work was divided.
This slide shows how the way teams are split sets the speed of work. The next slide shows why.

check.q: Why did a two-day coupon feature take three weeks?
check.a: The feature was split across three teams. At each handoff the ticket joined a queue, and that waiting ate the time.

slides.title: As the teams are, so is the system
slides.tldr: Conway's Law: a system is built along the lines of how the organization communicates, so system boundaries are a shadow of team boundaries.

blocks.title: Three cooks at a wedding
blocks.body: At a wedding, three separate cooks make the pasta, the roast chicken and the dessert. They talk little, so the pasta's sauce doesn't match the chicken's seasoning, and the joins between dishes are a mess. And two cooks who stand at the same stove end up blending their cooking into a single dish. The way the food divides follows the way the cooks divide.
A system's structure copies the communication structure of the organization that builds it.

blocks.caption: As the teams communicate, so the code is shaped
headers: What you see in the system

cells: Two teams work together every day
The code blends into one module
rows.tip: When people talk constantly they feel no need to respect a boundary, so the code has none either.

cells: A clear API and contract in the middle
rows.tip: Because they talk less, their agreement has to be written and clear. That pressure is what creates an API.

cells: Teams split by layer (UI, Backend, DB)
The system is split by layer too
rows.tip: The incident from the first slide. Every feature touches every layer, so every feature involves every team.

cells: That part belongs to everyone, so to no one
rows.tip: In ownerless code nobody refactors and nobody writes tests. In time it becomes the messiest part.

aside.title: The four-team compiler
aside.body: The line people repeat is: four groups building a compiler get a four-pass compiler. That wording is a later paraphrase. Melvin Conway's 1968 paper made the general point that a design copies the communication of the organization behind it. He offered it as an observation, not a rule, and it has kept holding true.

items.meaning: The line between two parts, where one part's responsibility ends and the other's begins.
Work passing from one team to another, with waiting and a risk of misunderstanding.

check.q: If two teams work in the same file every day, will a clear boundary form between them?
check.a: No. With constant contact they don't need a boundary, so the code blends together. A boundary forms only when the teams have to talk through a contract.

slides.title: The other way around: system first, then teams
slides.tldr: The inverse Conway maneuver: arrange teams along the architecture you want, with one owner and one written contract for each boundary.

blocks.body: If the law holds, you can use it in reverse: decide first how you want the system divided, then arrange the teams along those lines. This is the **inverse Conway maneuver**. In wedding terms: first decide which dishes you need, then give each dish one cook who is fully responsible for it.

blocks.caption: Five steps from the architecture you want to the teams you need

steps.title: 1. Draw boundaries
steps.body: By business area: Catalog, Checkout, Billing
steps.tip: Split by business capability, not by layer, so a feature can finish inside one part.

steps.title: 2. Give each an owner
steps.body: One team per boundary
steps.tip: Two owners for one boundary means no owner. A team may own several boundaries, but not the reverse.

steps.title: 3. Make teams full-stack
steps.body: UI to table, in the same team
steps.tip: With frontend, backend and data people in one team, a feature finishes without a handoff.

steps.title: 4. Write the contract
steps.body: An interface or API at the boundary
steps.tip: Other teams don't touch your internals; they talk only through the contract.

steps.title: 5. Measure
steps.body: How long a feature takes to finish
steps.tip: Watch whether lead time shrinks. If it doesn't, the boundary was drawn in the wrong place.

blocks.code:
# each module has exactly one owning team
/src/Catalog/    @shop/catalog-team
/src/Checkout/   @shop/checkout-team
/src/Billing/    @shop/billing-team

marks.tip: A pull request (a proposed change waiting for review) touching this path can't merge without the Catalog team's review. Ownership is written down here.

blocks.body: Why the contract matters: if Checkout reads Catalog's `Product` entity directly and Catalog renames its `price` column, Checkout breaks and two teams must change together, which is the handoff all over again. The price of the fix: a contract is extra code to keep stable, and reorganizing teams is disruptive. With fewer than about 5 engineers, one team and a modular monolith is enough.

marks.tip: The Catalog team can change its internal tables freely; as long as this method stays the same, Checkout won't even notice.
The dependency is on the interface. If Catalog's entity or repository crept in here, the boundary would be broken.

items: Before a big reorganization, run a small experiment with one or two teams.
Draw boundaries a single team can handle (usually 5 to 9 people); if one is bigger, split it.

items.label: Monolith or microservices as teams grow
Ports and adapters at the boundary

check.q: In the inverse Conway maneuver, what is decided first: the teams, or the system's divisions?
check.a: The system's divisions. Teams are arranged along them, so the teams' natural communication produces the architecture you want.

slides.title: When teams and services don't line up
slides.tldr: Three teams on one service, or one team with eight services: both are wrong; and changing only the org chart doesn't change the code.

blocks.body: Many people think that splitting teams ends the problem. But if the team split and the code split don't match, friction remains. It's like three cooks trying to cook in one pot: one cook's spices ruin another's flavor. Below are four kinds of mismatch, each with its fix.

blocks.caption: Mismatch vs match: team and code boundaries

columns.title: What doesn't line up
items: Three teams commit to one service
One small team holds eight services
The org chart changed, the code didn't
Everyone edits an ownerless shared library
columns.tip: In all four cases the team split and the code split run along different lines, so work and responsibility spread out.

columns.title: What lines up
items: One service or module, one owning team
Services only as big as a team can understand
When teams change, the boundaries are redrawn
Shared code has an owning team too
columns.tip: Each boundary has one owner, and the boundary's size fits what the owner can handle.

blocks.body: One boundary, one owner. When the team changes, change the boundary.

items: Building microservices and assuming the teams are now independent. If one team changes every service, you only added network calls.
Splitting services without looking at team capacity. A team of 3 will struggle to run 10 services.

use: The team has grown and people keep stepping on each other
Feature lead time keeps getting stuck in handoffs
avoid: The team is under 5 people; a modular monolith is enough

check.q: After building eight services, every feature still makes one team change all of them. What went wrong?
check.a: The service boundaries don't match how the team actually works. Work that spreads across several services within one team means they are really one boundary, so keep them together or redraw the boundaries.

slides.title: Redrawing boundaries: eight services, three modules
slides.tldr: To redraw boundaries, list which services each recent feature touched; the ones that always change together become one module with one owner.

blocks.body: Ryan's team of three runs eight services, and every feature needs a pull request (a proposed code change waiting for review) in several of them. Don't guess where the real boundaries are; read them from history. Write down which services each of the last few features touched.

blocks.caption: Services touched by each recent feature, and the module they point to

rows.tip: One small feature changed four services, so four pull requests and four deploys.
The same group moved together again.
And again. Services that change together every time are one boundary drawn in the wrong place.
A second group that moves together.
It overlaps the receipt email on mail, so invoice, mail and sms are one group.
auth changes alone, so it already is a good boundary. Leave it.

blocks.code:
# before: 8 services, 1 team of 3. A coupon feature = 4 pull requests, 4 deploys
cart-service/    price-service/   coupon-service/  order-service/
invoice-service/ mail-service/    sms-service/     auth-service/

# after: 3 modules, the same 3 people. A coupon feature = 1 pull request
src/Checkout/        <- cart + price + coupon + order
src/Notifications/   <- invoice + mail + sms
src/Accounts/        <- auth

marks.tip: Four services that always changed together are now one module, called by plain method calls instead of network calls.

blocks.body: The price: merging takes weeks of real work (joining data, rewiring calls), and the modules now deploy as one unit. Keep a part separate only if it truly needs its own scaling or its own team. Re-run this check every few months, because the answer drifts as teams change.

items: The git history is free evidence: `git log --name-only` over the last three months shows which folders move together.
If a merged module grows beyond what one team can understand, split it where changes rarely cross, not by layer.

check.q: Every feature for months changed cart, price and order together. What does that tell you?
check.a: They are really one boundary. Merge them into one module with one owner, so a feature becomes one pull request instead of three.

slides.title: Rules on paper, code that quietly drifts
slides.tldr: If an architecture rule lives only in a document, the code drifts away from it unnoticed until the damage is big.

blocks.title: A diet chart vs weighing yourself daily
blocks.body: The doctor hands Ryan a diet chart and he sticks it on the fridge. There is no scale in the house, so nobody notices the weight creeping up. Six months later, at the checkup, he is 13 lb heavier. An architecture rule is that same chart: if nobody measures it, nobody knows how far the code has moved.

blocks.caption: Rule-breaking imports over nine months (nobody was measuring)

items.label: January
items.tip: At the start everyone follows the rule: nothing from Doctrine or HTTP inside the Domain.

items.label: March
items.tip: A few shortcuts in rushed features. Each one looks harmless on its own.

items.label: June
items.tip: Newcomers learn from the existing code. When they see shortcuts, they take shortcuts too.

items.label: September
items.tip: Now Domain and Doctrine are almost impossible to pull apart. Undoing it is a matter of months.

blocks.body: This team had decided at the start: no Doctrine or HTTP code inside the Domain. The rule was written on the wiki, and a few people remembered it in code review. But people forget, people are busy, and reviewers don't scrutinize every single import.

aside.title: Small shortcuts, big decay
aside.body: Nobody objected to any single shortcut, because on its own each one was small. But over nine months, 96 of them added up until Doctrine was welded into the Domain code. The danger never arrived all at once. It came in through a little daily drift.
What isn't measured drifts away, slowly.

check.q: The rule was on the wiki, so why did 96 violations pile up?
check.a: Nobody was measuring it automatically. When you rely on human memory and code review, small violations slip past and keep accumulating.

slides.title: Fitness functions: rules that test themselves
slides.tldr: A fitness function is an automated check that measures an architectural quality or rule and runs in CI. Break the rule and the build goes red.

blocks.body: **Evolutionary architecture** is an architecture that can change in small, safe steps and still keep its important qualities while it changes. The guard that keeps those qualities in place is the **fitness function**. Think of the bathroom scale: on every commit it measures for itself and tells you whether everything is still fine.

blocks.caption: A few rules and the automated guard behind each

rows.tip: Reads imports and class dependencies without running the code and checks them against the rule. A violation turns CI red.

cells: No more than 10 queries on the product list
rows.tip: When an N+1 sneaks in, the query count jumps and the test catches it at once, long before anyone complains about slowness.
This is a performance budget. When the budget is exceeded the pipeline fails, so nobody quietly accepts a slowdown.

cells: No security holes in old libraries
rows.tip: This is a fitness function too: the security quality is measured, and nobody has to remember to check it.

blocks.body: A rule that is not measured automatically is not a rule, just a wish.

items.meaning: An automated check that measures one architectural quality (speed, dependency rules, security) and reports pass or fail.
A speed limit, such as p95 of 300ms; if it is exceeded, the build fails.
A robot that runs your checks and tests on every change before it is merged. A red result blocks the merge.
95 out of 100 requests are faster than this number. It shows what slow-ish users feel, not just the average.
One query for the list, then one more query for every row in it: 50 products means 51 queries instead of 1 or 2.

check.q: What is a fitness function, and why is it better than code review alone?
check.a: It is an automated check of an architectural quality. It runs on every commit and never gets tired or busy, so it catches even small violations.

slides.title: Guarding with Deptrac and a query budget
slides.tldr: Describe layers (the Doctrine library too) and permissions in deptrac.yaml, put a query-count limit in PHPUnit, and run both in CI. A violation blocks the merge.

blocks.body: First, the dependency rules: three layers, one more box for the Doctrine library (it lives in `vendor/`, so Deptrac can't see it unless you name it), and a list of who may know whom. **Domain** knows nobody, **Application** knows only Domain, and **Infrastructure** knows both plus Doctrine.

blocks.code:
deptrac:
  paths:
    - ./src
  layers:
    - name: Domain
      collectors:
        - {type: directory, value: src/Domain/.*}
    - name: Application
      collectors:
        - {type: directory, value: src/Application/.*}
    - name: Infrastructure
      collectors:
        - {type: directory, value: src/Infrastructure/.*}
    - name: Doctrine
      collectors:
        - {type: classNameRegex, value: '#^Doctrine\\.*#'}
  ruleset:
    Domain: ~
    Application: [Domain]
    Infrastructure: [Domain, Application, Doctrine]

marks.tip: Doctrine lives in vendor/, outside src/. Without this box, a Doctrine import inside Domain would pass unnoticed.
`~` means Domain may not depend on any layer, Doctrine included. Import Doctrine here and Deptrac fails the build.
Infrastructure may use the inner layers and Doctrine, but never the reverse. Arrows point inward only.

blocks.body: Now the speed limit. If an N+1 or any extra query sneaks in, this test goes red immediately.

marks.tip: Without the profiler there is no way to know how many queries ran.
The limit is 10. If each of the 50 products triggers its own query, the count passes 50 and the test fails.

items.desc: Check the dependency rules; exit code is non-zero on a violation
Nightly load test with a p95 threshold

items: On the day you add a new rule, many violations will show up. Record the old ones in a Deptrac baseline file, block only new violations, then shrink the baseline over time.
Timing tests are flaky. In CI measure something stable like the query count, and measure time in a separate load test.

check.q: Why does ProductListBudgetTest measure the query count instead of time?
check.a: Time varies from machine to machine, so the test would sometimes fail for no reason. The query count is stable, and it is enough to catch a real problem like N+1.

slides.title: A violation caught, and the fix
slides.tldr: A developer maps a Domain class with Doctrine attributes; Deptrac turns CI red; moving the mapping to Infrastructure fixes it. Guard only rules worth the upkeep.

blocks.body: Rushed on a Friday, a developer puts Doctrine attributes straight on a Domain class. Without a guard it merges, and that is shortcut number 8 of the 96. With the guard, the same change fails CI within minutes.

marks.tip: This one import breaks the rule. Deptrac fails the build and names this file and line.

blocks.body: The fix is not to switch the guard off. Keep `Invoice` a plain PHP class and describe the mapping outside it, in Infrastructure.

blocks.code:
<doctrine-mapping
    xmlns="http://doctrine-project.org/schemas/orm/doctrine-mapping"
    xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:schemaLocation="http://doctrine-project.org/schemas/orm/doctrine-mapping
        https://www.doctrine-project.org/schemas/orm/doctrine-mapping.xsd">
  <entity name="App\Domain\Invoice" table="invoices">
    <id name="id" type="integer"/>
    <field name="amountCents" type="integer"/>
  </entity>
</doctrine-mapping>

marks.tip: The table and column mapping now lives in Infrastructure. The Domain class has no Doctrine import left.

items: Register the folder under doctrine.orm.mappings with type: xml, dir: src/Infrastructure/Persistence/mapping and prefix: App\Domain.
Start with two or three rules you would defend in a meeting. Every rule is one more thing to maintain, and a flaky one teaches the team to ignore red builds.

use: Layer rules, performance budgets and security checks that must hold for years
avoid: Matters of taste (naming, spacing): a code-style tool does that job
Rules nobody has agreed on yet: the build would fail for no good reason

check.q: In the story, which rule did the Friday change break, and how did the developer fix it without turning the guard off?
check.a: It broke "no Doctrine inside the Domain". The fix: keep Invoice a plain class and move the mapping into an XML file under Infrastructure.

slides.title: The last responsible moment: when to decide?
slides.tldr: Postpone hard-to-reverse decisions as long as waiting costs nothing, because that is when you know the most. But without a trigger, "later" never comes.

blocks.body: Having no plan is a problem, and so is over-planning. The **last responsible moment** is the final point after which not deciding starts to cost you. Decide before it and you decide with too little information; decide after it and you are late. You must book the venue before the invitations are printed, but the last dish on the menu can still change a few days before the wedding.

blocks.caption: Three moments to make a decision

columns.title: Too early
items: Installing Kafka (a heavy message server) before there is any problem
You pay to run and learn it, and the guess may be wrong
columns.tip: A decision made on guesses, with little information. If it proves wrong, you throw away something expensive.

columns.title: Just in time
items: Start with a small solution and keep measuring
Switch when the trigger is hit
columns.tip: A decision made just before the last moment has the most information, and the damage has not started yet.

columns.title: Too late
items: The queue is overflowing, yet "we'll look later"
Deciding in firefighting mode
columns.tip: The problem is already on fire, and now you decide in a hurry.

blocks.code:
framework:
  messenger:
    transports:
      # Today: MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN=doctrine://default (the database is the queue)
      # Trigger: over 1000 messages/min (about 17 a second) or lag over 1 minute
      # Then only the env var changes: redis://redis:6379/messages
      async: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%'
    routing:
      'App\Message\SendInvoiceEmail': async

marks.tip: The trigger is written down as numbers. 1000 messages a minute is about 17 a second: a busy day, not a crisis.
Changing the DSN changes the transport (doctrine://default to redis:// or amqp://) and no handler code. The decision is cheap, so it is safe to postpone.

blocks.body: Before you say "later", write down which number will make you look.

items: Postponing a decision without a trigger is just avoiding the problem.
The price of waiting: the database queue polls the database, so near the trigger it adds load. That is why the trigger sits below the danger zone.
Don't postpone decisions that are expensive to change (the data model, a public API) so long that you get stuck.

check.q: Why is it safe to keep Messenger on the database transport today and change it later, and how do you pick the "later" moment?
check.a: Changing the DSN switches the transport without touching the code, so the decision is cheap. Pick the moment with a measured number (such as message rate or lag), not with a feeling.

slides.title: What the design doesn't say is what bites
slides.tldr: Every design document describes the happy path. The breakages hide in the unstated assumptions, and a reviewer's job is to drag them into the open.

blocks.body: Ryan wrote the checkout design: "When the user presses Pay, we call the Payment API; on success the order becomes paid and an email goes out." It reads clearly and everyone nodded. But behind every sentence sits an unstated assumption, and any one of them can turn out to be wrong on some bad night.

blocks.caption: What the design says vs what it quietly assumes

rows.tip: In reality the API can be slow or never answer. With no wait limit, our own server hangs along with it.

cells: On success the order becomes paid
The news of success will always reach us
rows.tip: The money is taken, but the connection drops before the answer arrives. Now we don't know whether the charge happened.

cells: The email service is never down
rows.tip: If a failed email fails the whole order, an optional step is breaking the main job.
On a slow network people press two or three times. Each press is a separate request and the money can be taken several times.

aside.title: The Friday-night double charge
aside.body: Nobody in the design review asked, "What if Pay is pressed twice?" On a Friday night with a slow network, 17 customers were charged twice. No line of code was wrong. The mistake was an unstated assumption: "the user will press it only once."
The most dangerous sentence in a design is the one nobody wrote.

items.meaning: The version of events where every step works and every system answers on time.
A wait limit: after this many seconds we stop waiting and treat the call as failed.

check.q: Behind the design line "the Payment API is called", which unstated assumption is dangerous?
check.a: That the API always answers quickly. If it is slow or silent and there is no wait limit, our own server gets stuck too.

slides.title: The four-question checklist
slides.tldr: Ask four questions at every step: what if it fails, what if it arrives twice, what if it is slow, what if we run it again? A good review starts here.

blocks.title: The engineer who approves a house plan
blocks.body: Looking at a plan, the engineer doesn't say "lovely". They ask: what happens if a water pipe bursts? Where does the lift stop in a power cut? Will the foundation take two more floors? They didn't build the house, so their eyes are on the bad days. A design reviewer is exactly that engineer.

blocks.caption: The four questions at each step, and what a good answer looks like

cells: timeout + fallback + the states written down
rows.tip: The money was taken but the order isn't paid. Who repairs such in-between states must be written down.

cells: double click, a message delivered twice
rows.tip: Will the result stay the same if the same job arrives twice? If not, money, emails or stock will be hit twice.
Waiting is the most expensive thing: one slow system holds the threads of the others and slows everyone down.

cells: What if we run it again?
rows.tip: A retry is the same request sent again. If running the job twice isn't safe, the retry is itself a new accident.

blocks.body: At every arrow ask: what if this step fails, arrives twice, is slow, or is run again?

items: Ask the four questions of your own design too. It's hard to spot mistakes in what you wrote yourself, so keep the questions written down.
Ask questions, don't pass verdicts: instead of "this is wrong", say "what happens if the charge succeeds but we time out?"

items.meaning: Safe to do twice: the second run leaves things exactly as the first did, like pressing a lift button again.
Waiting a little longer before each new retry (1s, 2s, 4s) instead of hammering a struggling system.
Thousands of clients retrying at once, which buries a system that was only slow.

check.q: Why ask "what if we run it again?" separately, when "what if it arrives twice?" is already covered?
check.a: Arriving twice has an outside cause (the user, the messaging system). Running again is our own decision (a retry). A retry needs its own thought about unknown outcomes and retry storms.

slides.title: A design review, hands on
slides.tldr: Ask the four questions of the happy-path checkout code to find four gaps, then fix the code for each and write review comments that carry the question.

blocks.body: This is the code behind Ryan's design. Run your eye over it with the four questions in hand: where is there no timeout, where can it run twice, and where does a slow email hold up the whole job?

marks.tip: No timeout and no Idempotency-Key. A slow answer will hang the server, and a retry or double click can charge twice.
If the mail server is slow or down, the request fails even after the money was taken. The email could have been sent later.
Give up after 3 seconds of silence and 5 seconds in total (max_duration). A slow API can't hold the whole server hostage.
Every order gets one fixed key. If the same order arrives twice, or we ask again after a timeout, the Payment API doesn't charge a second time.
A timeout means we don't know if the money was taken. We neither mark it paid nor failed; it stays pending, and asking again with the same key is safe.
The email goes to the queue. If it fails, Messenger retries it on its own, and the customer's order is not held up.

blocks.title: The three parts of a good review comment
items: The question: "If Pay arrives twice, what reaches the Payment API?"
The risk: "The money could be taken twice and the customer will complain."
The suggestion: "Could we send an Idempotency-Key?"
This code still has a small gap: if flush succeeds but the process dies before dispatch, the email is lost. The full fix is an outbox.
The `pending` answer only parks the order. To settle it you still need a status check or a webhook (the payment system calling us back), or a retry with the same key.

items.label: Saving the DB and the message safely together: outbox
After a timeout the outcome is unknown

check.q: In the good code, why was the email moved out of the request, and in answer to which question?
check.a: "What if it is slow or fails?" A slow or failing email no longer holds up the order, and the queue retries it.

slides.title: Pre-mortem: stage the failure in advance
slides.tldr: A review fails when everyone looks only at the happy path. In a pre-mortem you assume the project has already sunk, then hunt for the reasons.

blocks.body: Design reviews often fail because everyone shares the author's enthusiasm and nobody wants to ask the awkward question. A **pre-mortem** breaks that pressure. A post-mortem happens after the death; a pre-mortem happens before: "Imagine it is six months from now and the project has sunk. Why did it sink?" Raising fears is now the assignment.

blocks.caption: The five steps of a pre-mortem, about 30 minutes in all

steps.title: 1. Jump ahead
steps.body: "Six months from now, the project has failed."
steps.tip: Treat failure as something that already happened and people say "because" instead of "what if", and the fear drops.

steps.title: 2. Write alone
steps.body: Everyone writes reasons for 5 minutes
steps.tip: Writing alone first stops the loudest voice from taking over the whole discussion.

steps.title: 3. Pool them
steps.body: Gather everyone's list in one place
steps.tip: A worry that lived in one head is now in front of everyone.

steps.title: 4. Vote
steps.body: Which are the likeliest and most damaging?
steps.tip: Not all risks are equal. Weigh likelihood and damage together and pick the top three.

steps.title: 5. Assign work
steps.body: One owner and one remedy for each
steps.tip: Without an owner and a remedy it is just a list of worries. The design changes only when work is assigned.

blocks.code:
Assume: six months from now the checkout project has failed.

Reason                         Likelihood  Damage  Owner   Remedy
Money charged twice            high        high    Ryan    Idempotency-Key
Payment API slow, server hung  medium      high    Kevin   timeout 5s, circuit breaker
Email failure fails the order  medium      low     Laura   email via queue

items: Attacking the person, not the design: "Why didn't you think of this?" Ask instead, "Has this been considered?"
Spending hours on small things (names, formatting) while the hard-to-reverse decisions (data model, API) slip by.
Commenting and then going quiet. A review isn't finished until every risk has an owner and a remedy.

items.meaning: A switch, like a fuse, that stops calling a failing service for a while so it can recover and we stop wasting waits.

use: Before finalizing a big or hard-to-reverse design
Before adopting a new technology or a new integration
avoid: Small decisions you could change in one afternoon

check.q: Why does a pre-mortem say "the project has sunk" rather than "the project might sink"?
check.a: When failure is treated as having happened, people feel safe saying what they fear and why. With "might sink", optimism pressure keeps everyone quiet.

slides.title: The service that is wired to everything
slides.tldr: When business rules are tangled directly into Doctrine, an SMS vendor and a payment client, tests are slow and switching a vendor is misery.

blocks.body: In Kevin's `OrderService`, the rule for confirming an order, the database save, the SMS and the payment call all live in one class. To test one tiny rule (a coupon lowers the price), you need the database, the SMS vendor and the payment server. The test takes 4 seconds, and when someone asks to switch SMS vendors, you have to touch 40 files.

blocks.caption: Testing one rule drags in four things

nodes.label: Rule test
nodes.tip: All we want is to check one business rule, yet everything else comes barging in.

nodes.label: OrderService
nodes.tip: Rule code and equipment code share one class. Change one and the other breaks.

nodes.label: Doctrine
nodes.tip: The service calls EntityManager directly. Without a real (or equivalent) database, the test can't run.

nodes.label: Twilio client
nodes.tip: The vendor's name sits inside business code. Switching vendors means rewriting this class.

nodes.label: Payment client
nodes.tip: Running the test makes real network calls: slow, and sometimes it even charges money.

edges.label: The test only wants to run one rule.
To run the rule, it reaches into the database.
Then it calls the SMS vendor's SDK.
Then it makes a network call to the payment server too.

aside.title: The 40-file SMS switch
aside.body: To cut costs, the team decided to switch SMS vendors. It should have been an afternoon's job, but the vendor's SDK was spread across 40 services. It took two weeks, and two old rules broke along the way.
When business rules and equipment code are tangled together, tests get slow, switching vendors gets hard, and the rules themselves get hard to understand.

items.meaning: An outside company whose service you pay for, such as an SMS or payment provider.
The ready-made code kit a vendor gives you for calling its service from your program.

check.q: Why does testing the coupon rule need a database, SMS and a payment server?
check.a: Because the rule's code is wired directly to all three. If the rule lived on its own, you could run just that part and test it.

slides.title: Ports and adapters: the phone's charging port
slides.tldr: The rules sit in the middle and ask the outside world for things through interfaces (ports). The database, SMS and HTTP are adapters of those interfaces, and dependencies point from outside in.

blocks.title: A phone's charging port
blocks.body: What a phone does inside and where its power comes from are two separate things. The phone only decides what its port looks like (USB-C). Chargers, power banks and laptops all shape themselves to fit. The phone has no idea which company generated the electricity in the wall. The inside defines the port, and the outside adapts to it.

blocks.caption: Rules in the middle, outside equipment plugged into ports through adapters

nodes.label: Controller
nodes.tip: Calls the rules from the outside world. This is called a driving adapter.

nodes.label: Domain + use case
nodes.tip: The most important part, in the middle. No mention of Doctrine, Symfony or any vendor here.

nodes.label: OrderRepository
nodes.tip: The rules state what they need, in business language. They don't know who will provide it.

nodes.label: CustomerNotifier
nodes.tip: A contract for notifying someone. SMS, email or push: to the rules they are all the same.

nodes.label: DoctrineOrderRepo
nodes.tip: Fulfills the port's contract with Doctrine. This class knows the port, but the rules don't know this class.

nodes.label: SmsNotifier
nodes.tip: Fulfills the port's contract with Symfony Notifier. Switch vendors and only this class changes.

edges.label: calls
asks via interface
implements
asks via interface
implements

blocks.body: Dependency arrows point from the outside in. The rules never know the equipment.

items.meaning: An interface written by the inner rules: "I need someone to do this for me", in business language.
A class that fulfills a port's interface and talks to Doctrine, SMS or HTTP.
The inner rules don't depend on outer classes; the outer classes depend on the inner interface.
One class that carries out one thing a user wants, such as confirming an order, by calling the rules and the ports in order.

aside.body: The rules define the interface, the equipment fulfills it, never the other way around.

check.q: In dependency inversion, who depends on whom, and why is that the opposite of what you'd expect?
check.a: The adapter depends on the port, not the rules. Normally you'd expect the rules to depend on the database; here the dependency is turned around.

slides.title: Ports, use cases and adapters in Symfony
slides.tldr: Write the interface on the inside, inject it into the use case, and write the Doctrine or Notifier adapter on the outside. `#[AsAlias]` lets autowiring match them up.

blocks.body: First, the rules' side: two ports and one use case. Nothing from Doctrine or Symfony is `use`d here.

marks.tip: Written in the inside's language: get and save. No QueryBuilder or EntityManager anywhere.
The use case knows only interfaces. Who stores the order or who sends the SMS, this class has no idea.
The rule lives in confirm() on the inner Order. The use case only sets the sequence: fetch, change, save, notify.

blocks.body: Now the outside. Two adapters fulfill the ports' contracts, and `#[AsAlias]` tells Symfony which class serves which interface.

marks.tip: This one line teaches autowiring: whenever OrderRepository is requested, hand over this class. No YAML needed.
When nothing is found, it throws a business-language exception (OrderNotFound), not a Doctrine null or error.
The SMS goes through Symfony Notifier's TexterInterface. To switch vendors, change the DSN.

items: Keeping Doctrine mapping attributes on the Domain entity is a practical compromise. If you want it fully clean, use XML mapping and keep the entity free of attributes.
A controller or a Messenger handler is a driving adapter: it only turns a request or message into a command and calls the use case.
The price: every outside thing needs one interface and one adapter. Here that is 4 extra classes for one use case. It pays off with complex rules or changing vendors, not plain CRUD.

items.label: The older way of splitting layers

check.q: Who injects OrderRepository into ConfirmOrderHandler, and how?
check.a: Symfony's autowiring. The Doctrine adapter carries `#[AsAlias(OrderRepository::class)]`, so the container supplies it for that interface.

slides.title: Testing without a database, swapping a vendor in one class
slides.tldr: An in-memory fake of a port makes rule tests run in milliseconds, and a new vendor just means one new adapter class.

blocks.body: Because the port exists, a test needs no real database: a plain fake class holding an array is enough. Back to the phone: for a test, you skip the wall socket and clip on a small battery instead, and the phone still runs.

marks.tip: A plain array stands in for the database. save() puts the order in; get() takes it out.
The spy only remembers whom it was told to notify, so the test can check it later. No SMS is actually sent.
No database, container or network. Only the rule runs, so the test finishes in milliseconds.

blocks.caption: Switching the SMS vendor: what changes and what doesn't

columns.title: What changes
items: composer require symfony/vonage-notifier (the new vendor's bridge)
The SMS DSN: twilio://... becomes vonage://...
Your own adapter class, only if no bridge exists
columns.tip: Only the outside equipment. That is all you have to change.

columns.title: What stays the same
items: Order and its rules
ConfirmOrderHandler
All the rule tests
columns.tip: Everything inside stays exactly as it was, and its tests need no changes.

aside.body: Test the rules with fakes; test the real equipment less, in separate integration tests.

items: Give each adapter its own integration test (the Doctrine adapter against a real database, say), so you know it really fulfills the port's contract.

items.meaning: A simple stand-in with tiny working logic, like an array instead of a database.
A stand-in that remembers what it was asked to do, so the test can check it afterwards.
A one-line address string, like twilio://ID:TOKEN@default, that tells Symfony which outside service to use.

check.q: What do you gain, and what do you lose, by running rule tests on InMemoryOrderRepository instead of a real database?
check.a: The test runs in milliseconds and needs no database. You lose verification of real Doctrine behavior, which the adapter's own integration test covers.

slides.title: The port that leaks the equipment's name
slides.tldr: When QueryBuilder or a vendor type shows up in a port, the inside gets tangled with the equipment again. Name and type the port in business language.

blocks.body: Creating an interface doesn't make something hexagonal. If database language seeps into the interface, it is a port in name only. A phone port stamped "this company's charger only" is no longer a port.

marks.tip: Return a QueryBuilder and the use case builds queries itself. Doctrine has crept back inside the rules.
Switch SMS vendors and this method is dead. A port that carries a vendor's name isn't independent any more.
The name is business language: "awaiting payment". How the query is done is the adapter's private business.

blocks.body: Name and type your ports in the language of the business, not of the equipment.

items: Creating an interface for every class. Where change is unlikely and testing is easy, the class itself is enough.
Applying full hexagonal to a small CRUD app. It pays off only when you have complex rules or vendors that change.

use: You have complex business rules that change often
You may switch vendors, or use more than one
avoid: Plain CRUD with no real rules

check.q: Which goal of hexagonal architecture fails when a port returns a `QueryBuilder`?
check.a: Keeping the rules separate from the equipment. Once the use case works with Doctrine's types, it is tangled up with Doctrine again.

slides.title: The business speaks one language, the code another
slides.tldr: When the business and the developers don't use the same words, misunderstandings seep into the code. A ubiquitous language is one shared vocabulary, and the code uses it too.

blocks.body: The head of the business said, "When an order is canceled, no refund, just store credit." Ryan built a refund. Two weeks later it emerged that the business uses "canceled" in two senses: if the customer cancels, it's credit; if we cancel, it's a refund. All the code said was `setStatus(3)`, and nobody knew which cancellation a 3 meant.

blocks.caption: What the business says vs what the code says

cells: Only the author knows what 3 means
rows.tip: The business sentence and the code sentence don't match, so neither a newcomer nor the business can read the code.

cells: What does a negative balance mean?
rows.tip: The business calls the same number credit and the code calls it debt. When words don't match, the rules go wrong too.

cells: The coupon has been used up
After how many uses is it "finished"?
rows.tip: The rule ("can be used only once") isn't in the code; there is just a counter.
Flags with meaningless names pile up until the code is a puzzle.

aside.title: The price of two "cancels"
aside.body: Because of the wrong refund, about 300 customers got money back who shouldn't have. There was no bug in the code: it did exactly what the developer understood. The mistake was in the understanding.

items.meaning: The business or field of work the software is being built for.
The person who understands that business best, usually a staff member or business owner, not a developer.

check.q: The code ran fine, so why did 300 customers get a wrong refund?
check.a: Because "canceled" had two meanings and nobody separated them. The code did what the developer understood, not what the business needed.

slides.title: Turn the business sentence into a method name
slides.tldr: Give each business sentence its own method, named in the business's words, with the rule inside. A refund after a customer cancellation then looks wrong at a glance.

blocks.body: Back to Ryan's order. The business has two sentences: "when the customer cancels, they get store credit" and "when we cancel, they get a refund". Store credit is money kept in the customer's account for the next purchase; a refund sends the money back. The fix is one method per sentence, named in those exact words.

marks.tip: Is 3 "canceled by the customer" or "canceled by us"? Only whoever wrote it knows, and a month later even they may not.
Always refunding is right for one cancellation and wrong for the other. This is how about 300 customers got money they should not have.
The business sentence "the customer cancels" is now a method. Whoever reads the code reads the same words the business says.
One shared guard: an order that is already canceled or shipped can't be canceled again.
Store credit is added; there is no refund call here. A refund on this path would stand out in review.

blocks.body: Name the method the way the business says the sentence.

items: Inventing the words yourself. Take them from the business person, or you have created a third language.
Renaming the whole codebase in one go. Add the new method, move callers one at a time, then delete `setStatus()`.

use: Rules the business talks about out loud: cancel, refund, approve, expire.
avoid: Plain CRUD screens with no business rules, where `setName()` is perfectly fine.
The price: time with a domain expert up front, and renaming old code.

check.q: Where, in the new code, can a reviewer see that a customer-canceled order must not be refunded?
check.a: In the handler: `cancelByCustomer()` is followed by `addCredit()`, never `refund()`. The method name carries the business rule, so a wrong refund looks wrong at a glance.

slides.title: Bounded context: one word, one meaning, one boundary
slides.tldr: In a big system the same word means different things in different places. Draw a boundary (a bounded context) around each meaning, and keep one meaning per word inside it.

blocks.title: Three kinds of "order" in a pizza place
blocks.body: At the cash counter, an "order" is a bill with prices and payment. In the kitchen, the same "order" is a list of what to cook in which oven. To the delivery driver, an "order" is a box with an address. All three are right, because each holds one meaning inside their own job. The trouble starts when all three share one table: the kitchen renames an oven column, and the cash counter's bill stops working.

blocks.caption: The same word "order", three meanings in three contexts

rows.tip: Each context keeps inside "order" only what its own job needs.
Instead of one giant 60-column Order table, three small, clear models in three contexts.
The reasons for change differ, so in separate contexts a change in one doesn't break another.
An easy start: each context gets its own folder and namespace, with its own Order class. They talk only through ids or events.

marks.tip: The message crosses the boundary carrying an id and dish names only. Prices and coupons stay inside Sales.
Kitchen turns the message into its own Order, with only what it needs to cook. It never reads the Sales tables.

blocks.body: One word, one meaning, inside one context. Change the context and the meaning may change.

aside.body: Not one giant Order, but a small Order of its own in each context.

items: Sit with the business people, write down their own words, and use exactly those words as class and method names.
Contexts talk through ids or events, never by reaching into each other's database tables.

use: The same word means different things to different teams or jobs.
avoid: A small app with one team and one meaning per word: a single model is simpler.
The price: some data lives in two places, and you write hand-off code between contexts.

check.q: If Sales and Kitchen share a single Order class, what trouble lies ahead?
check.a: Each team will change the class for its own needs, and one team's change will break the other's code. The class will pile up fields for every meaning and become huge and confusing.

slides.title: Entity and value object
slides.tldr: An entity is recognized by its identity (id), a value object by its value. Make things like money and addresses value objects and the rules become safe on their own.

blocks.body: A $10 bill can be swapped for any other $10 bill, because all you care about is the value. That's a **value object**: no identity, equal values mean the same thing, and once created it never changes. But your Social Security number and mine are different, even if we share a name. That's an **entity**: it has an identity (an id), and it's the same person even when everything else about them changes.

marks.tip: A private constructor: you can't push in just any value. You have to create one through a named static method.
Money is stored in cents (an integer). With floats, 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, which is terrifying in money math.
plus() doesn't change itself; it returns a new Money. That is immutability: once created, the value never changes.
The id is fixed once and never changes. The Customer stays the same even if the name or phone changes.
Money is stored right in the customer table, in the columns credit_cents and credit_currency. It needs no table or id of its own.

items: Money, addresses, date ranges, emails: these are usually value objects. If "are these two equal?" is decided by looking at the values, it is a value object.
Avoid primitive obsession: use an `Email` class instead of `string $email`, so an invalid value can't even be created.
Storing money as a float. Store an int in cents, or use a dedicated money library.

check.q: Two Customers have the same name, phone, everything. Are they the same entity? And what about Money(500) and Money(500)?
check.a: Customer: no, if the ids differ they are different entities. Money: yes, equal values mean the same value object.

slides.title: What goes wrong with float money and raw strings
slides.tldr: A float or a raw string accepts anything, so mistakes slip in silently. A Money or Email object refuses wrong values at the door.

blocks.body: A **float** is how a computer stores a number like 19.99: very close, but rarely exact. Convert $19.99 to cents with `19.99 * 100` and you get 1998.9999999999998, and `(int)` cuts it to 1998. One cent vanishes on every sale of that item. Over 100,000 sales that is $1,000, and no error appears anywhere.

marks.tip: The float 19.99 is stored as a close-but-not-exact value, so times 100 lands just under 1999 and (int) throws the rest away.
Nothing says one number is dollars and the other euros. The sum is meaningless, and PHP raises no error.
A plain string accepts anything. The broken address is saved, and the first welcome email fails later, far from here.

blocks.code:
$price = Money::cents(1999);            // integer from the start: exact
$total = $price->plus(Money::dollars(5)); // 2499 cents, exact

$total->plus($feeInEuros);              // DomainException: $feeInEuros is EUR

Email::fromString('ryan@');            // InvalidArgumentException: can't exist

marks.tip: The price enters as whole cents, so there is no float and no conversion to get wrong.
Adding different currencies is refused inside Money::plus(), exactly where the rule belongs.
An Email value object checks the format in its constructor, so an invalid one can't exist in the first place.

blocks.body: Never store money in a float. Store whole cents, inside a Money.

items: Percentages still need a rounding rule: 5% of 1,999 cents is 99.95 cents. Decide how to round, and test it.
Several currencies, taxes and exchange rates: use a library such as moneyphp/money instead of growing your own.

use: Any amount you add, compare or store: prices, balances, fees.
avoid: A number nobody does arithmetic on, like a likes counter: a plain int is enough.

check.q: `(int) (19.99 * 100)` returns 1998. Why does it, and what is the fix?
check.a: The float 19.99 is not stored exactly, so times 100 lands just under 1999 and `(int)` cuts it. Keep integer cents from the start, inside a Money object.

slides.title: Aggregate: the boundary that guards the rules
slides.tldr: Make the things that change together into one aggregate and let its root guard the rules. If outside code changes the inner parts directly, the rules break.

blocks.body: An order has rules: at most 20 items, and once confirmed nothing can change. Rules like these are called **invariants**: things that must always be true. In the code below the rules are scattered around the controller, so it is easy to break them from somewhere else.

marks.tip: The order already had 20 lines and this made 21: nobody checked the limit. If another controller or command does the same, the rule will be broken for sure.
Even an empty order could be confirmed. Nobody is guarding the rule.
The only way to add an item. The rules live inside this method, so everyone has to obey them.
Instead of holding a Product directly, it keeps only a ProductId; there is no need to reach inside another aggregate.
confirm() checks for itself whether the order is empty. With no setStatus(), this guard can't be bypassed.

blocks.caption: From outside, you can only enter through the root's door

nodes.label: Controller
nodes.tip: Only calls the public methods of the aggregate root. It never touches the inner OrderLine directly.

nodes.label: Order
nodes.tip: The guardian of the rules. Every change goes through its methods.

nodes.label: OrderLine
nodes.tip: It has no separate existence without Order. Only Order creates and changes it.

nodes.label: Product
nodes.tip: A separate boundary. Order keeps only its id, not the whole object.

edges.label: Calls addLine(), and the rules are enforced.
Creates the OrderLine, within the rules.
Holds on to only the ProductId.

blocks.body: To change an inner part, go through the root's door. Change only one aggregate per transaction.

items: A giant aggregate: put everything under one root and transactions grow and locking gets painful. Keep them small.
Pushing DDD into every little class. Use an aggregate only when you have complex rules; plain CRUD doesn't need it.

items.label: How a repository becomes a port

check.q: The code has `confirm()` but no `setStatus()`. How does that protect the invariant?
check.a: confirm() checks the condition inside (the order isn't empty), and it is the only way to change the status. Nobody outside can change the status and skip the check.

slides.title: When checkout calls everyone itself
slides.tldr: If you finish a job and then call everyone else one by one, adding anything new means touching checkout, and one slow service slows everybody.

blocks.title: The headmaster going from room to room
blocks.body: To announce a holiday, the headmaster walks into each classroom and tells them one by one. When a new class opens, he has to remember to go there too. And if he gets stuck in one classroom, all the others wait. Here the headmaster is the checkout code, and the classrooms are Inventory, email and Loyalty.

blocks.caption: Checkout calls three places itself, and if one fails they all fail

nodes.label: Checkout
