nodes.tip: Taking the order is its real job, but it has been forced to keep track of everyone else.

nodes.label: Inventory
nodes.tip: When an order is placed, stock must change. Checkout calls it directly.

nodes.label: Email service
nodes.tip: It can be slow or even down, yet checkout waits for it.

nodes.label: Loyalty
nodes.tip: A less important feature, but its slowness or breakage holds up the whole order.

edges.label: Checkout calls Inventory itself.
Then it calls the email service.
Then it calls Loyalty.
If Loyalty fails, the order itself gets stuck.

blocks.body: Now the business wants "tell analytics when an order is placed, too." The checkout file has to be opened again and tested again. The work grows, and so does the risk each time. Add up the customer's wait too: Inventory 50 ms, the email service 800 ms, Loyalty on a bad day 3 seconds. That is nearly 4 seconds at the spinner for an order that was saved long ago.

aside.body: If whoever finishes the job calls everyone else itself, everyone is tied to it: adding something new is hard, and one service's slowness is everyone's slowness.

check.q: Why do you have to open the checkout file to add analytics, and why is that a problem?
check.a: Because checkout calls everyone itself. Anything new means touching the core code again, and every touch is a risk to something as important as placing an order.

slides.title: Event-driven: pin it to the notice board
slides.tldr: Event-driven means that when the work is done, you just announce what happened. Whoever cares listens and does their own job, and the announcer never needs to know who they are.

blocks.body: This time the headmaster pins a notice on the board: "Holiday tomorrow." Whoever needs it reads the board and does their own part: class teachers tell the parents, the office changes the timetable. When a new class opens, the headmaster has nothing to do. In software, that notice is called an **event**: a fact written in the past tense, like `OrderPlaced`, saying "this has happened."

blocks.caption: Sales only announces; the listeners do their own jobs

nodes.label: Sales
nodes.tip: Does only its own work, then makes an announcement. It doesn't know who is listening.

nodes.label: OrderPlaced
nodes.tip: The notice board. Its name is in the past tense because it is a fact, not an instruction.

nodes.label: Inventory
nodes.tip: Hears the announcement and sets stock aside by itself.

nodes.label: Notification
nodes.tip: Hears the announcement and sends the email by itself. If the email fails, Sales couldn't care less.

nodes.label: Loyalty
nodes.tip: Hears the announcement and awards points by itself. Adding a new listener like this means no change to Sales.

edges.label: Sales announces: an order has been placed.
Inventory hears it and sets the stock aside.
Notification hears it and sends the email.
Loyalty hears it and adds the points.

blocks.body: An event is a fact about the past ("an order was placed"), not an instruction ("send an email").

Now count the customer's wait. Before: 50 ms + 800 ms + 3 s, about 4 seconds. After: only the saving of the order, about 50 ms. The three jobs run behind the scenes, in a worker (a separate program that picks jobs up and does them), and a failed one is retried without anyone watching the spinner.

items.meaning: A fact written in the past tense (OrderPlaced) that has already happened and can't be changed.
The code that hears an event and does its own job.
All the parts don't agree right now, but they will after a short while.

check.q: In an event-driven design, do you have to touch the Sales code to change Loyalty's rules, and why?
check.a: No. Sales only announces OrderPlaced and doesn't know who is listening. Loyalty just changes its own handler.

slides.title: CQRS: the checkout log and the catalog
slides.tldr: CQRS splits writing (rules) from reading (speed) into separate models. A list page that needed 21 queries becomes one flat query.

blocks.title: The library's checkout log and its catalog
blocks.body: A library lends and takes back books in the checkout log, where the rules are strict: does the member have a card, has the last book come back? But readers go to the catalog to find a book, sorted by subject and quick to search. The two jobs differ, so the layouts differ. That is CQRS: the **command** (write) side enforces the rules, and the **query** (read) side shows things fast.

blocks.caption: Writing guards the rules; reading only has to be fast

columns.title: Command: the write side
items: Place, cancel, confirm orders
Enforce the rules in the Order object
Returns only success or failure
columns.tip: Rules and invariants matter here. Correctness comes before speed.

columns.title: Query: the read side
items: Order lists, dashboards
Pre-arranged for the page
Changes no data
columns.tip: Speed and convenience matter here. There are no rules to enforce, so it stays simple and flat.

marks.tip: The order lines are lazy-loaded to compute the total. 1 query for the orders + 20 for their lines = 21 queries to show 20 rows.
Not a Doctrine ORM entity, but the DBAL Connection directly. Reading needs no rule-laden objects, so there is no hassle of building them.
order_summary is a pre-built flat read model, with every column the page needs and no joins. One query for 20 rows, instead of 21.

blocks.body: The price: a small handler listening to `OrderPlaced` must keep `order_summary` in step, and for a moment after an order the list may not show it yet. For a small app, one plain query is enough; add the split when a page measurably hurts.

aside.body: CQRS is a split: the write model is for rules, the read model is for speed.

items: The simplest step: same database, but separate command handlers and query classes. That alone gets you most of the benefit.
The next step: a separate read table, updated by listening to events. That is where eventual consistency comes in.

check.q: Why does the CQRS read side read a flat table directly instead of building rule-laden Order objects?
check.a: Reading doesn't have to enforce any rules. Reading straight from a flat, pre-arranged table saves the joins and the cost of building objects, so it is faster.

slides.title: Events and handlers in Symfony
slides.tldr: Create separate command.bus and event.bus in Messenger, make events small past-tense readonly classes, and let listeners hear them with #[AsMessageHandler].

blocks.body: First, the two buses and the async transport (the queue the events wait in). The event bus is fine with no listeners at all (`allow_no_handlers`), because when you make an announcement you don't need to know who is listening. Routing `OrderPlaced` to `async` means its handlers run in a worker you start with `php bin/console messenger:consume async`. Without a running worker, events just sit in the table.

blocks.code:
framework:
  messenger:
    default_bus: command.bus
    buses:
      command.bus: ~
      event.bus:
        default_middleware:
          enabled: true
          allow_no_handlers: true
    transports:
      async:
        dsn: '%env(MESSENGER_TRANSPORT_DSN)%' # .env: doctrine://default?auto_setup=0
        retry_strategy: {max_retries: 3, delay: 1000, multiplier: 2}
      failed: 'doctrine://default?queue_name=failed'
    failure_transport: failed
    routing:
      'App\Sales\Event\OrderPlaced': async

marks.tip: An event bus with no listeners is not an error. Once the announcement is made, the announcer's job is done.
The async transport: a queue stored in your database here. Retries 3 times, waiting 1 s, 2 s, 4 s.
Events that fail all their retries land here, so they are not silently lost. Inspect them with messenger:failed:show.
OrderPlaced goes to the async transport, so the announcer answers the user right away.
The name is OrderPlaced, not PlaceOrder. An event gives information; it doesn't give orders.
Sales only announces here. It doesn't know which handlers exist, and it doesn't need to.
Inventory wrote its own handler. Adding a new listener means no change to the Sales files.

items: Stuffing all the data into an event and making it huge. Put in the id and the essential facts; listeners can look up the rest themselves.
With async, the same event can arrive twice, so handlers must be idempotent.

check.q: Why is "OrderPlaced" in the past tense, and not an instruction like "PlaceOrder"?
check.a: An event is a fact that has already happened; listeners can't be forced to act on it, but they can know about it. "PlaceOrder" is an instruction, a command, which has one specific recipient.

slides.title: A crash between save and announce loses the event
slides.tldr: If the server dies after saving the order but before dispatching the event, nothing is announced. Store the event in the same database transaction and send it from a worker.

blocks.body: Look again at `PlaceOrderHandler`: it saves the order, then dispatches `OrderPlaced`. Two steps, and the server can die between them (a deploy, an out-of-memory kill). Order 4821 is saved, but no stock is set aside and no email goes out. Nothing logs an error, because the line that failed never ran.

blocks.caption: Broken: the order is saved, then the process dies

actors.label: Order handler
actors.tip: The PlaceOrderHandler running inside the web request.

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Where the order row is stored.

actors.label: Event bus
actors.tip: Where OrderPlaced should have been sent.

blocks.caption: Fixed: the event is stored with the order, and a worker sends it

actors.label: Database
actors.tip: Holds both the orders table and the messenger_messages table, on one connection.

actors.label: Worker
actors.tip: A separate process run by messenger:consume. It delivers stored events.

messages.label: One transaction: save order, store OrderPlaced
messages.tip: Both rows are written inside the same BEGIN ... COMMIT.

messages.note: Stock reserved, email sent. If it dies, the message is retried

blocks.code:
framework:
    messenger:
        buses:
            command.bus:
                middleware:
                    - doctrine_transaction

marks.tip: Wraps the whole handler in one database transaction. The async transport uses the same connection (doctrine://default), so the stored event commits or rolls back with the order.

blocks.body: The price: delivery is at least once, so a handler can run twice and must be idempotent. Events now arrive after a short worker delay. This only works because the queue lives in the same database as the orders; with RabbitMQ or SQS the save and the send are two systems, and you need a real outbox table plus a relay. If losing an event is harmless (say, analytics), plain dispatch is fine.

items.desc: run the worker that delivers events
see events that failed all their retries

check.q: Why does storing the event in the same transaction as the order stop events from being lost?
check.a: The order and the event commit together or not at all, so there is never a saved order without its event. A worker then delivers it, and retries if it fails.

slides.title: When it pays off, and what it costs
slides.tldr: Event-driven and CQRS loosen boundaries and add speed, at the price of harder debugging, eventual consistency and more code. Adopt them only once the need is proven.

blocks.caption: The benefits, costs and when to adopt each approach

cells: Scale and shape reads and writes separately
rows.tip: Both are techniques for "separating". One separates a job from the jobs that follow it; the other separates reading from writing.

cells: Hard to see who listens; debugging
Keeping two models in sync; more code
rows.tip: Press one button and you can no longer see in one place what happened. You can't manage without logs and tracing.
Right after placing an order, it may not show up in the list yet. The UI has to handle that wait.

cells: Events arriving twice, ordering, schema changes
Mismatch from mistakes updating the read table
rows.tip: Handlers must be idempotent, and an event's shape must be changed carefully, because other teams depend on it.

cells: Many parties act on the same event
Read load is far higher than write load
rows.tip: You need evidence: say 5 listeners on checkout, or a list query that has become slow.

cells: A job of two or three simple steps
rows.tip: Adopt it from day one and you pay for the extra complexity without any benefit.

blocks.title: Three questions before you adopt
items: Do several parties really do separate work on one event?
Aren't simpler steps (such as a separate query class on the same database) enough?
Can our team handle the cost of eventual consistency and debugging?

blocks.body: Event-driven and CQRS are not free magic. Adopt them once the pain is proven.

use: Many parties do separate work on the same event
Read load and write load grow at different speeds
avoid: A simple CRUD app with a small team
Instant consistency is essential (such as a balance)

aside.title: Event sourcing is a different thing
aside.body: Many people think CQRS automatically means event sourcing. It doesn't: event sourcing means storing data as a list of events rather than as the current state. You can use CQRS and event-driven design on their own. For event sourcing in detail, see [[workflows/event-sourcing/why-is-it-200|Event sourcing]].

check.q: Why is it wrong to bolt CQRS and event-driven design onto a small CRUD app?
check.a: There is nothing to gain (one party, low load), yet you pay for eventual consistency, extra code and harder debugging from day one.

slides.title: The newcomer's question nobody can answer
slides.tldr: If a system's structure and the reasons behind its decisions live only in people's heads, the knowledge leaves when they do. Three tools capture it: C4, sequence diagrams and ADRs.

blocks.body: Kevin is new at the company. He asks, "Why does the report service have its own MongoDB when everything else is PostgreSQL?" Nobody on the team is sure: the person who made the decision left two years ago. There is a photo of a whiteboard, but nobody knows what the boxes or the arrows mean. Kevin wonders, "What will break if I remove this?" and it takes him a week to find out.

blocks.caption: What the code does is in the code; these three are not

columns.title: What lives in heads, not on paper
items: Which parts the system is made of
Who calls whom, and how
Which decision was taken, and why
columns.tip: You can't learn these three by reading the code, and they walk out the door with the people.

columns.title: What survives when written down
items: C4 diagram: the parts and how they relate
Sequence diagram: what happens in order
ADR: why this decision
columns.tip: Each question has its own tool. All three are short, and can live in the repository.

aside.title: After the removal
aside.body: In the end someone removed MongoDB and moved the data to PostgreSQL. Two weeks later they found that one report query had been built specifically for MongoDB's aggregation pipeline, and the whole report had become 12 times slower. If the reason had been written in an ADR, a week of searching would have taken a minute.
Code tells you what the system does. Only writing tells you why.

check.q: Why can't you tell the reason for a decision just by reading the code?
check.a: Code shows what was done, not why. The reasons, the alternatives and the constraints live in people's heads, so they have to be written down separately.

slides.title: C4: four zoom levels, like a map
slides.tldr: C4 draws a system at four levels: Context, Container, Component and Code. It works like zooming a map, and each diagram shows exactly one zoom level.

blocks.title: Zooming into a map
blocks.body: On a map of the United States you first see the country and its neighbors. Zoom in and you see states and highways, zoom further and you see the streets of a neighborhood, and finally the floor plan of a single house. Each zoom answers a different question, and if you cram every level onto one map, you can read nothing. C4 works the same way.

blocks.caption: The four levels of C4, zooming in from top to bottom

layers.label: Level 1 — Context
layers.sub: the system, its users and outside systems
layers.tip: The country map. Even non-technical people get it: what our system is and who it talks to.

layers.label: Level 2 — Container
layers.sub: the runnable parts: apps, databases, queues
layers.tip: The district-and-city map. A "container" is a separately running part, and doesn't have to be Docker.

layers.label: Level 3 — Component
layers.sub: the main parts inside one container
layers.tip: The neighborhood map. For example the Catalog, Checkout and Billing modules inside a Symfony API.

layers.label: Level 4 — Code
layers.sub: a class diagram; you can usually skip it
layers.tip: The floor plan inside the house. Code changes fast, so this diagram goes stale. If you need it, generate it from the IDE.

blocks.caption: Each level, in the example of an online shop

cells: Customer, admin, payment gateway, SMS vendor
rows.tip: The internal technology isn't shown here, only the outside relationships.

cells: Vue app, Symfony API, PostgreSQL, Redis, worker
rows.tip: Each box carries its technology, and each arrow carries its protocol (JSON/HTTPS, SQL).

cells: The team working on that container
Catalog, Checkout, Billing inside the API
rows.tip: The module boundaries you set up earlier show up here.

cells: A class diagram, generated automatically if needed
rows.tip: A hand-drawn class diagram goes stale in weeks. If you want one, generate it with a tool.

blocks.body: One zoom level per diagram. And every box gets a name, a responsibility and a technology.

items: For most teams the Context and Container diagrams are enough. Draw a Component diagram only where the inside is complicated.
Put a verb on every arrow ("reads and writes", "sends order events"), not just an inked line.

check.q: To explain the system to a new PM, which C4 level do you show first, and why?
check.a: Context. It has no internal technology, only our system, its users and outside systems, so it can be understood without knowing the technology.

slides.title: Sequence diagram: what happens in order
slides.tldr: C4 shows who knows whom; a sequence diagram shows what happens in what order, including the failure branch that box-and-arrow pictures miss.

blocks.body: A C4 diagram is a map, and a map has no time in it. But the answer to "what happens if the money is taken and then we time out?" comes in time order. So draw one sequence diagram for one checkout scenario, and show the failure branch alongside the happy path.

blocks.caption: Checkout: the success path and the timeout path

actors.label: Vue app
actors.tip: The part that runs in the user's browser.

actors.label: Symfony API
actors.tip: Runs the checkout rules and calls the Payment API.

actors.label: Payment API
actors.tip: An outside service. We have no control over its answer.

messages.label: charge + Idempotency-Key
messages.tip: Each order gets one fixed key, so a retry doesn't charge twice.
This is the branch box-and-arrow pictures miss, and where most mistakes hide.

messages.label: 202 verification in progress
messages.tip: We don't know whether the money was taken, so we say "verification in progress", not "confirmed".

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Vue app
    participant A as Symfony API
    participant P as Payment API
    U->>A: POST /checkout
    A->>P: charge + Idempotency-Key
    alt success
        P-->>A: 200 paid
        A-->>U: 201 order confirmed
    else timeout
        P--xA: no answer
        A-->>U: 202 verification in progress
    end

marks.tip: `alt` ... `else` ... `end` shows alternative branches of one path. The happy and the failing one sit in the same picture.
`--x` is an arrow that never reached its destination: no answer came.

items: One diagram, one scenario. With more than four or five participants, split it into two pictures.
Name messages with real API names (`POST /checkout`), not vague ones like "process order".
Mermaid lives in the repository as text; GitHub or GitLab renders the picture itself, and changes show up in the pull request.

check.q: Even with a C4 container diagram, why do you need a separate sequence diagram?
check.a: A container diagram has no time in it: it shows who knows whom, not the order or the failure branches. Questions about timeouts and retries are answered by order.

slides.title: ADR: the record of a decision
slides.tldr: An ADR (Architecture Decision Record) is a short file with the context, the decision, the alternatives and the consequences. Once written it is not edited; a new ADR supersedes an old one.

blocks.body: Think of a court ruling: an old ruling isn't erased, a new ruling overrides it. An ADR works the same way. Each big decision gets a one-page file with a number, like `docs/adr/0007-email-via-messenger.md`. When someone later asks why, the answer is right there.

blocks.code:
# ADR-0007: Send email asynchronously through Messenger

Date: 2026-03-14
Status: Accepted

## Context
Sending the email at checkout takes 4 seconds on average. When
the email service is slow or down, the order fails too. The team
is 4 people, with nobody to run a separate queue service.

## Decision
Send emails to a worker through Symfony Messenger's doctrine transport.

## Alternatives rejected
- RabbitMQ: not needed yet, and costly to run.
- Sending inside the request: the slowness and failures remain.

## Consequences
+ The order no longer depends on how slow the email is.
- Email arrives a few seconds late; the worker must be kept running.
Revisit: if we pass 1000 messages a minute, look at RabbitMQ.

marks.tip: Status: Proposed, Accepted, or Superseded by ADR-0021. The old one isn't deleted; only its status changes.
Context: what problem, what constraints. Use numbers: not "slow" but "4 seconds".
Alternatives rejected and why: when someone in the future raises the same idea, the answer is here.
Consequences, good and bad both, and the trigger for when to revisit the decision.

blocks.code:
# ADR-0021: Move the email queue to RabbitMQ

Date: 2027-04-09
Status: Accepted
Supersedes: ADR-0007

## Context
ADR-0007 said to revisit at 1,000 messages a minute (about 17 a
second). We now see 1,200 a minute.

## Decision
Send emails through RabbitMQ. The Messenger message classes stay.

## Consequences
- One more service to run and watch.
+ Handles the load; the switch is a transport config change.

--- and in docs/adr/0007-email-via-messenger.md, only this changes:
Status: Superseded by ADR-0021

marks.tip: The new file points back at the one it replaces, so a reader can follow the chain in either direction.
The only edit to the old file. Its context and reasons stay, so the history reads: doctrine transport then, RabbitMQ now.

blocks.caption: An ADR's life cycle: once Accepted it isn't edited, only superseded

nodes.label: Proposed
nodes.tip: A draft, discussed in a pull request.

nodes.label: Accepted
nodes.tip: The team has agreed. From now on the text of the file is not edited.

nodes.label: Superseded
nodes.tip: A new ADR was written that replaces the old one. The old one stays as history.

edges.label: team agrees
things change

items: Editing an old ADR to record a new decision. The history is lost, and nobody knows when or why things changed.
Writing ADRs for small decisions. Write them only for hard-to-reverse or contested decisions.

check.q: When a decision changes, what do you do instead of editing the old ADR, and why?
check.a: Write a new ADR and set the old one's status to "Superseded by ...". That keeps the history: when the decision changed and why.

slides.title: Documents that go stale
slides.tldr: A wiki diagram drifts from the code and goes stale in two years. Keep diagrams and ADRs beside the code in the repository, and they get updated in the same pull request.

blocks.body: The most common mistake: a beautiful picture drawn in Confluence or Google Slides, far from the code. The code changes, the picture doesn't, and within two years it starts to lie. A stale document is worse than none, because people believe it. The fix: make diagrams files like code, and keep them in the repository.

marks.tip: Containers inside a softwareSystem: the second level of C4. The names, responsibilities and technologies of the boxes are all in the file.
The relationship verbs are in the file too. Change one line of the file to change an arrow, and the picture updates itself.
The tool builds the picture from this view, so nobody draws boxes by hand.

blocks.title: Rules for keeping documents fresh
items: Diagrams and ADRs live in the code repository, in the `docs/` folder.
A change to the picture goes in the same pull request and the same review as the code change.
Validate the diagram files in CI, so a broken file can't be merged.

items.desc: Check that the DSL file is valid

aside.body: A document that isn't next to the code won't live as long as the code.

items: The price: CI can check that the file is valid, not that it is true. In review, ask "did this change touch the picture?"
A small team can start with a Mermaid file: GitHub renders it and there is no extra tool to install.

items.meaning: A shared website where a team writes pages, like Confluence. It sits apart from the code, so nothing forces it to change with the code.

check.q: Why does a picture drawn in a wiki go stale faster than diagram-as-code in the repository?
check.a: When changing code, nobody remembers to open the wiki and update the picture. In the repository the diagram file is reviewed in the same pull request, so it goes stale less.
